title: Much Better than the Cheaper, Slider Types of Gauges
text:
Every other tire gauge I have ever used has a straight bar type with a sliding measure that blows out the bottom to show the pressure. This gauge by TireTek is a lot different and brings more features to the table than those simpler gauges.

First things first - this gauge is much, much larger than any other I have used with the sole exception of one built into an air compressor. The entire (no pun intended) assembly is over a foot long and it has a huge dial gauge on the end. The dial is encased in rubber and this serves two purposes - it protects the dial and it makes the dial assembly look a bit more like a tire.

The dial is very easy to read and it gives a clear reading accurate to within 1 PSI. The range goes from 0 PSI up to 60 PSI in graduations of one. There’s no rocket science here.

Where this gauge adds more is in the pressure release button which you press and hold to slowly release some air from the tire. As you hold it down and the air escapes, the pressure dial slowly drops to show the current pressure so you can stop at any point you like.

I like that fact that even though the joint near the dial is somewhat loose and the unit can be turned about it does not leak air.

This is a well-made gauge. The hose and casing are heavy rubber and will resist most simple cuts and scuffs, and when it is stored properly the rubber should not degrade. The dial is heavy and though it has a plastic face it is solid and can survive a decent drop. The joints between the hose and the metal connector fittings do not leak which is good for maintaining accuracy.

This is a great tire gauge. It’s a solid unit, easy to use and easy to read. It works a lot better than the slider types, too.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Lightweight and Inexpensive
text:
Polarized sunglasses are very useful for cutting down reflected light. I use them when I go fishing to cut down on the glare coming off the surface of the water on sunny days. I have used multiple pairs of polarized sunglasses and this pair is a good one, particularly when considering how inexpensive they are.

This is a very lightweight pair of glasses and they feel like they weigh nothing when they are being worn. They are half-frames so they cut down on the amount of material and add some style to them at the same time. They are mostly black with yellow trim. They came in a semi-hard crush-resistant case which is a nice touch.

One of the main concerned I had was build quality. I have used other sets of inexpensive sunglasses and they have been flimsy or have broken outright after a short time. These seem to be better made than that. They have a little flexibility to them and the hinges and nose piece are attached with tight screws. There is no play in the hinges. And, the lenses are attached correctly and do no jiggle at the corners like I have seen with other half-frame solutions.

The polarization is excellent and is aligned properly (which can be tested against an LCD computer screen). When they are held level they provide light reduction as expected. As they are rotated polarized light fades until it is almost completely dark at 90 degrees.

Overall these are nice sunglasses and they seem to be made very well. The price on these is very low too and that makes them a good deal.

title: Weatherproof Flashing Marker - Lots of Uses!
text:
Lights and reflectors are a good method of attracting attention, either to alert of the need for caution or to draw specific attention to a specific place like a driveway. Solid reflectors are common in rural areas and are used to mark road entrances. This solar flasher is an excellent way to draw attention to drivers and people on foot as well. Having spent time living on a farm I can see numerous possibilities.

This is a cylindrical light, 2.75" in diameter and about 3" tall (just counting the reflective red light enclosure) and is capped by a solar panel. It collects light during the day and when the light level gets sufficiently low it beings to flash. The flash is very bright but is not blinding and it can be seen clearly at a distance.

The base of the light has a pressure clamp that is tightened by a single screw. It can accommodate a pole approximately 2" in diameter, less if using a padding material like rubber insulation. So, this will work for some fence posts - if you intent to mark a fence, measure the pole diameter to ensure this light will clamp properly or plan to add an extra pole to account for it.

The light’s switch is located under the base and is a small, black slider. This is smart placement as it is hard to mess with once the light has been affixed in place. It does mean that if you want to turn off the light it must be unmounted from wherever it has been placed.

This light is completely sealed and is waterproof so it can be left outside regardless of the weather.

One thing I am not sure of yet is the effective run time. I have not tried to run it all night but it does run for a good while from what I have determined in testing. I also have not yet determined the full charge time when it has been run down. So far it has shown no signs of weakening.

I can see numerous uses: marking the entrance to a road or driveway, alerting to the edge of water, marking a structure on a body of water like a boat house or buoy, indicating the corner of a fence, marking a dangerous structure like a parked piece of heavy equipment, and when used with multiple units can mark a trail. This fall, it will be used to mark our flag as we navigate a cornfield maze at one of the local farms. There are many other ideas for this light; this is just a few possibilities.

This is a fine flashing light that works well and requires zero maintenance. It gathers solar energy so it does not require a power source, it flashes very brightly when operating and it is sealed to keep moisture out. Overall, I am pleased with it.

title: Can Restore and Recondition Even Old Leather Work Gloves
text:
Wild Bill's Leather Conditioner is a product designed to restore and revitalize leather goods. This is a product suitable for shoes, purses, car interiors and more. This was the first time I have worked with it.

I tried the conditioner on a pair of leather work gloves I cleaned with the leather cleaner. This is a milky white liquid that, unfortunately, does not have a particularly pleasant smell. This leather conditioner seems to work well. I gave it a tough test - restoring a leather work glove that has seen years of use - and it made the glove softer and more supple. Based on my experience with it, I can recommend it as a good solution for reconditioning leather goods.

title: Cleans Deep Stains and Dirt
text:
In the past I had never used a cleaning solution just for leather, relying mainly on a heavy cloth and warm, soapy water. Wild Bill's Leather Cleaner was my introduction to a dedicated leather cleaner, and I was curious just how well it worked so I gave it two very solid tests - a pair of leather dress shoes I have had for about 20 years and a pair of heavy leather work gloves that have been used for everything from electrical work to hauling tree branches.

To be fair, the leather shoes may be old but they are in relatively good shape, just in need of cleaning. The gloves, however, are atrocious and are stained with worn-in dirt.

The leather cleaning solution is a cloudy white solution that actually has a pleasant smell, somewhat like lemon-scented dish detergent. This was a very pleasant surprise - I expected a harsh chemical smell. As a bonus, the fragrance is not strong so it does not require use in a ventilated area. I added a little to a clean, soft cloth and set to work on the shoes. The shoes are not brand new and considering their age I did not expect miracles; that said, the leather cleaner did a great job of removing surface dirt and dust and made the shoes look years younger than they really are - far better than my damp cloth with soapy water ever could.

The miracle was in how well the cleaner worked on the leather heavy work gloves. Originally a warm shade of tan, the palm of my gloves have been dirtied to an ugly gray (and the fingers are even worse). I applied the cleaner to the cloth again and rubbed in a circular motion in the middle of the palm. It took some work but most of the dirt lifted as I scrubbed. It's not perfectly clean but the palm of my glove looks a lot better than it did!

Wild Bill's leather cleaner does an excellent job of cleaning and rejuvenating leather surfaces. I used it on a particularly soiled article and it cleaned that surface better than I could have asked. This is an excellent product.

title: Needs several significant improvements, then it could be a great product
text:
I was excited for this product as I’ve been using a corded compressor to fill my car tires for many years. I was hoping this could replace it. Out of the box the inflator is solid and appears well engineered. The screen is large, and the buttons are of good size and quality. Also, the packaging and protective pouch have a very premium feel to them. And I double checked the pressure readings with a digital bike tire gauge (which I’ve found to be accurate) and the pressure readings matched up. So there are a lot of positives.

However, the negatives far outweigh these positives as this tool has a very specific job and it wasn’t working out for me. Once I started using it, several flaws became readily apparent. First, the hose isn’t very long, so if a valve is near the middle or top position on the wheel, the inflator just dangles by the hose or you have to bend over and hold it the entire time. I’m not going to turn my car on just to spin the wheels to a better position that doesn’t strain the hose or the valve stem. This is one big problem. The next major problem is that the pressure kept overshooting the preset. I had it on 36 psi, and it kept inflating long after it hit 36, and it went to 37 (my bike gauge read 37.4, so it wasn’t a rounding artifact). I don’t know why it wouldn’t stop when it got to the preset. I tried one tire on 35 psi, and it automatically stopped at 35, and soon after it reached 35. But it overshot the 36 psi preset twice (and the second time it happened I counted to 15 between when 36 appeared on the screen and when it turned off). Relatedly, I wish this had a pressure release button. The only way to lower the pressure was to unscrew the hose, let air out, and then reattach the hose to check the pressure. This button wouldn’t be as necessary if the pump turned off when it was supposed to.

Overall, the cordless convenience of this inflator does not make up for the additional hassle of using it to inflate my car tires. I’m sticking with my tried and trusted corded inflator.

title: good quality, might get stolen
text:
I ordered the valet edition to protect my car from being both dinged by my neighbor (on opening their doors) and scraped as well (they park by Braille). I am very pleased with the quality of the item--feels light but solid, with pretty strong magnets.
I have three critical comments:
1) the security wire could be cut by a thief with a good pair of clippers; the wire will only protect against unprepared opportunist thiefs. Since I have an outdoor urban parking space, there is a substantial risk--but it's one I'm willing to take.
2) I applied a thin plastic door-rim protector to my car doors (so I don't ding my neighbor's car). It is difficult, but not impossible to close the door over the security wire with that door-rim-protector in the way. Luckily, I have a 5-inch space near the door-handle with no rim-protector, and that's where I try to stick the wire usually. If your door-rim-protector is continuous and thicker, you may be forced to cut away a small portion of it so you can close the wire in the door. When I close the door with the wire hitting the door-rim-protector, it slightly damages the plastic coating on the wire; this is something to keep an eye on, as an uncoated wire could cause slight scratches to the car here and there.
3) The suction cups on the security wire seem pointless. I could not get them to stick at all; it would be impractical to try each time I reattach the door shox. Further, they are unnecessary and make the door shox security wire look somehow cheaper and more vulnerable (more tempting). I don't use them. I would prefer large hooks on the end of the wire instead so I could hook it to my inside-door-handle; that would make installation easier, and the precise form of security would be somehwhat hidden.

Despite these issues, I think it's a good product. I am willing to buy another set if these get stolen. Now I can ask my neighbors to fix our car without worrying they'll just redamage it again.

title: Taken off on the first day.
text:
We used to have Britax sunshades to keep on the two middle windows, but they've lost their clinginess this past year. My wife drives our daughter to daycare in the mornings, and the route has the sun shining directly onto their faces, so we needed replacements immediately.

I installed this one on the left window just to test it out. The clips on the top are somewhat thin, and I thought they'd break off eventually. However, I did like that this shade covered more of the window than our previous Britax ones did.

When I closed the door after successfully installing the shade, though, I heard the plastic clatter against the window. I thought it was the window at first, so I immediately removed the shade and reapplied it. Sure enough, it made the same noise. I found out that it was the plastic bar that was hitting against the window when I closed it, but thought it wouldn't be a big issue.

When I came home from work, I noticed the shade was on the floor of the car. I asked my wife later if she didn't like it--"No." Apparently the clatter against the window keeps occurring whenever driving, and the noise became annoying. My wife had a guest in the car that day, and she too commented on how annoying that noise was.

So, unfortunately, while the shade does cover a bit more, we're going to have to rely on the tinting already installed on our windows for adequate sun block rather than suffer the clanging noise.

I would say it does its job a bit faster than the other clay I usually use. One other notable fact I noticed. It doesn't mare(sp?) the clear coat as much as other brands. Which means if your paint is pretty good to start. A simple wax is all that is needed to get the slippery wet look everyone wants. Other Clay's have often need a bit diminishing compound or polish to fix what the clay did to the clearcoat. So far this clay has been very gentle on the dozen or so cars I used it on.

While i paid for this and have not had any compensation. I would be pleased to try other items from this company/seller. For the cars i deal with in Ohio. This has been a very pleasant surprise that it worked better than the pricier brands. I would highly recommend you try this brand.

And to help those who are not aware of good techniques to use clay. Wash the vehicle all over and rinse. Leave wet. With fresh soap and water. Soap entire vehicle(soapy vehicle won't spot if it dries before final rinse). With soapy vehicle and clay in hand. Rub clay on surfaces (start on top and finish on lower rocker panels, it also works on glass). After each panel, knead the clay (or twist to reveal fresh clay). Add soapy water to always have a wet soapy work area. Don't worry if the areas you clay dry out, the vehicle will rinse in the end. You will know you did a good enough job when you no longer feel debris on the paint as slide you wet hands on the surface. Once the vehicle leave is rinsed and dry. Evaluate the amount of scratches or spiderwebing and polish/wax with your favorite products.

title: The Light Has Gone Out...FINALLY!!!!!
text:
Nearly 4 years ago, I had the opportunity to buy a 3 year old used VW Passat for an excellent price. I bought the car and loved it...for about the first 3 months. Then, the 'check engine' light came on for the first of MANY times and things went downhill rapidly.

I quickly learned from other VW owners that the cars are very sensitive and the 'check engine' light comes on for any little reason. I can confirm this as one of the MANY times my light came on, it was due to a speaker wire being loose. I like knowing when there is or about to be an issue with my car, but the 'check engine' light for a speaker wire is ridiculous.

I had a garage that I used and trusted with my car for awhile. But each time the 'check engine' light came on in my VW, I had to take it across town to be fixed. They'd hook the car up to their computer and tell me what was wrong and what needed repair. And each time, I'd take their word for it and shell out the money to fix the issues. In my state, the 'check engine' light cannot be on when a car is inspected or it immediately fails. Naturally, my light was on each time the car was inspected so I had to shell out money to get the light off and the car to pass inspection.

The garage I was using had been recommended by a friend and so I trusted it. The guys were full of pity each time I had to drop the car off for yet another repair. They even cut me some slack a few times on the bill. What fantastic people, right? Silly, naive me. When I had to buy 2 catalytic converters only 18 months apart, I finally got suspicious and stopped going to that garage. I found another closer to home that I like and so far, trust.
But now, I don't just have a new garage, I have an extra layer of protection. My 'check engine' light has been on for months and I've been ignoring it. Inspection isn't until September, so I figured I'd worry about the light then, however, I've been trying to stash away some money here and there to prepare for September's inspection costs. Last week, I got the Launch 4001 Creader Check Engine Light Reader. As soon as it arrived, I immediately went outside to my car in the rain (OK, light drizzle) and hooked it up. Actually, plugged it in is a better description as that's all I had to do. To my excitement, only ONE error code came up and it was for something very minor. The Launch Check Engine Reader gave me the option to turn the 'check engine' light off! Let me say that again...the Launch Check Engine Reader GAVE ME THE OPTION TO TURN THE CHECK ENGINE LIGHT OFF!!!!!!!!!! AND I DID!!!! The always annoying orange light is GONE, BABY GONE!!! (Sadly, I am sincerely this excited to have the 'check engine' light gone!) I wish that I had never waited so long to get the Launch Check Engine Light Creader, but better late than never. I am beyond thrilled to have it! It couldn't be any easier to use. Trust me...if I could do it, EVERYONE can. As I mentioned, I do have a garage for repairs/inspection that I'm comfortable and satisfied with, but I also have my Launch Creader as well, so I will know for certain what is truly wrong with my car. I already have 3 friends and 1 family member who want to borrow it to check their own cars as well!

Unless I win Powerball, I am going to own this car for a few more years. It is truly a relief to know that having the Launch Creader will give me the peace of mind of knowing exactly what is wrong with my car and how much it should cost before the car even goes to the garage for repairs or inspection. No more getting ripped by the garage either. And best of all, I can turn off that annoying orange light on my own now! The Launch Check Engine Creader is a MUST HAVE for anyone out there who has a car with a 'check engine' light that comes on each time they sneeze! I LOVE this and am beyond thrilled to have the Launch Check Engine Creader. Wish I would have bought it sooner, but better late than never!

text:
**UPDATE: February 15,2021**
I'm just updating my review to say that I have now had these installed on my truck for the last 8 years and they are still in perfect condition! I would upload new pictures, but they still look the same! These have been a fantastic purchase for my truck and worth every single penny!

**UPDATE: December 30, 2013**

These visors are still going strong. I did decide to have them paint matched to my truck (see picture in customer images). They took to the paint prep job and new paint very well. I had to remove the 3M tape that came installed on them when I gave them to the paint shop and re-applied new 3M tape when I got them back and re-installed them on my truck. No sticky residue was left on any of the visors or in my window tracks (AVS uses good quality 3M automotive grade tape on these!). Reapplying the new 3M tape went smoothly and they have been holding true since April (eight months now) with no issues. I still highly recommend these visors!

**Original review from February 19, 2013**

Vehicle installed on: 2012 Ram 1500 Laramie CC

I purchased the AVS visors off Amazon as they were the best price I could find and I got them delivered in two days with my Prime membership.

I have only had the tape on version in the past (on my '99 Tahoe) and although I was quite pleased with them, I swore I would not tape anything to the paint on my new $45k truck.. LOL! So I bought these in-channel visors.

I must say they are rather simple to install. I only had issues with the passenger front door.. it wasn't seating right and kept engaging the auto-down window feature. After about fifteen minutes of cussing and wanting to break it in half, I finally got it wiggled into place. All windows are up and will stay that way for at least a few days to ensure the tape takes and all visors seat properly. Including my rant fest with the one window, this install took me approximately twenty-five minutes for all four windows.

Now that they are installed.. I am not sure if I should have them paint matched. (I know they are taped in.. but I could always put fresh 3M tape on them after being painted to install them again.) Decisions, decisions. I would recommend these visors to everyone!

To previous reviewers who have had issues with installing these visors due to the window auto-down feature:

These visors do fit our trucks (please verify the part number is applicable to your specific vehicle) and they will install into windows with the auto-down feature. Please do not rate this item poorly due to your lack of patience!

You have to be *patient* with the installation.. the visors will not seat perfectly at first and you will most likely have a few minutes of frustration when the auto-down feature of the windows is engaged due to making contact with the inside edge of the visors. Once you get them installed, leave your windows up, uninterrupted, for at least 24 hours. This allows the visors to properly seat into position.

It finally warmed up enough for me to tape on my tailgate cover. I know that chrome is not liked by everyone but I think it adds that touch I was looking for to finish off the rear end view of my truck.

I bought the Putco/Mopar part for this.. not some cheap knock off. Having plenty of other Mopar (genuine OEM) chrome accents already on my truck, I can confirm that this part truly does match the OEM chrome perfectly! It installed quickly and easily (wiped the OEM handle with an alcohol pad, did a dry placement test, peeled the tape strips off and pressed it into place.. then repeated with the moveable handle cover - all less than five minutes).

I have noticed that my rear view camera is a little haloed now (pictures are posted in customer images).. but it does not block any of the view that matters (on-coming traffic or pedestrians). No more troublesome as the red glow my Recon Xtreme Light Bar gives off at night.. but just thought I'd mention it to anyone who may be considering this mod.

title: It fits with the rest of them.
text:
I was afraid this wouldn't work well with the Smittybilt engine/transmission, and transfer case skid plates that I already had. It did without any modification to it or the others. I saw one review that mentioned the directions state that the original fuel tank cover (skid plate) has to be removed. It doesn't. The directions don't state that it does. You have to remove various original bolts to bolt this on. Follow the directions, even though they're not perfect, they aren't wrong. I cleaned the original and sprayed some black paint over the surface rust that was there. I'd recommend using rust-conversion paint, but I didn't have any on hand, and I was too lazy to go get any.

I used a floor jack to support the plate while bolting it up. The directions mention using a jack stand. A bottle jack or scissor jack would work too. Use a block of wood to keep from scratching the paint. It'll get scratched later, but nobody likes scratching something new.

The only issue I had was that bolt holes in the original sheet metal cover shifted a bit when the bolts were removed. It's sheet metal. There are built in stresses, and stress from this skid plate fitting tightly over it. After a bit of prying I managed to get the bolt holes to all line up. If you've never done anything like this, don't freak out when that happens. It's normal.

If it wasn't 95º at 10 pm this wouldn't have been hard at all. I'm fat, 63 and hold a steering wheel all day. Don't get in a hurry and you won't have any real problems.

title: Absolutely Solid

One of the main reasons I got this is because the basket I have mounts behind the stock tire carrier, and it fits exactly the same as it did on this. Without the basket mounted, the new LT285/70-17 spare worked just fine. With the basket mounted, it didn't (it barely held a stock tire anyway), and I had to add an extension. Even with the extra leverage, it barely vibrates when I close the tailgate.

The only issue I had with installation was getting the washers and nuts onto the back side of the bolts while mounting the tire carrier. Welded nuts would make installation a touch easier, but would add cost, and make adjustment impossible.

The instructions were easy to follow, and were sufficiently illustrated. I wish all Jeep accessories had instructions like these. Just make sure you don't miss a step and you'll be fine. If you choose to use the 3rd brake light extension, you might need longer leads. I don't need it, but the stock wire was barely long enough for the brake light without the extension.

Your mileage may vary, but I'd buy this again. If I had another Wrangler.

title: So, I won't mention the horrible packaging this time.
text:
I installed this with the engine/transmission skid plate. I can see just installing that one, but not just this one. They really work together. I reviewed it also, as well as the evap canister plate.

The fitment problem: Making something that fits 10 years worth of different Jeep Wrangler models can't be easy. Every mounting hole but one on this plate is slotted. One of the holes is so adaptable it requires a large flat washer to cover it. One hole is just a hole. In my case, on a 2016 Wrangler Sport 2-door, I slotted that hole. Either it and 4 of the others worked, or the other 5 worked and it didn't. I drilled another hole near it, and cut between it and the new hole with a Dremel cutoff wheel to join them, then ground the sides smooth and painted it. So, now the plate fits fine. Every hole has a bolt, and every bolt has a hole. Honestly, I can't take a star off for that.

Is it indestructible? Absolutely not. Nothing is. Does it offer increased protection? Absolutely. Is there something better out there? Probably, but it likely won't work as well with Smittybilt's engine/transmission skid plate, and it probably costs more. This is all I needed. I'm not going out to try to break my Jeep.

See. I didn't mention that it almost fell out of the box Smittybilt put it in, or how badly it was packaged.

If you don't and you want to keep your stock front bumper, you still might consider this instead of nothing, which is what the plastic that's there is. If you want a more aggressive appearance, this ain't it, buy a bumper with a skid plate made for it that looks meaner than hell and weighs half a ton.

-
Rugged Ridge should lead with the modifications you'll have to make to newer JKs built after 2010. They're buried so far down in the instructions that an average person would already know this won't fit, having partially installed it, before finding out they'll have to drop it back down and cut the frame. It's not quite trivial, though what needs to be cut off is most likely an artifact of assembly. I used a grinder because I had one. On the other hand, if you don't ever want to drill a hole to install something on your Jeep, don't ever install anything on your Jeep.

-
Myself, I'm trying to keep the stock bumpers and mostly stock appearance of my 2016 2-door Wrangler Sport, while protecting those things that aren't protected. So far that's included Smittybilt engine/transmission and transfer case skid plates, EAG rock sliders, and now this. It's better protection than the plastic that was there, and in fact, it might be possible to put the plastic back over it, maybe, though it'll just get torn off later.

text:
I bought this to protect the transmission cooling lines, because any reasonably large stick could take them out. If you ever plan to take your Wrangler off road, you need this or something like it for that reason. I installed it and the transfer case skid plate on my 2016 2-door Wrangler Sport today. Stock suspension.

Don't completely ignore the lift kit requirement. I checked clearance between the front differential and the left front brace with the suspension on the left side compressed within 1/4" of the stop, and it clears. With a hard landing that actually bumps the stop, it might hit, it might not. I'd already planned on a 2.5" lift, and I don't plan on driving it hard off road, so I risked it. Another model might not clear.

Otherwise, installation was easy enough, though a bit of manual dexterity is required. YouTube videos are a major help. The included instructions, not so much. One star off for packaging. Smittybilt simply doesn't box their skid plates well enough.

I've written a review of the transfer case skid plate also, and the evap canister plate. I really couldn't see not getting all three. Can these be bent? Absolutely. These are good enough for my purposes.

title: It Works
text: I was too lazy to go to a store and buy this after I finally found the leak in my Jeep Wrangler's spare, so I have no clue about value. I used to work in a tire shop, and plugs haven't changed much, though the plugs sold in stores at one time were actually strips of solid rubber that didn't work as well as this seems to have. If it's hard to get the reamer in the hole, this will fix it. Make sure to ream the hole out until the reamer doesn't require a lot of force. I wasted one "string" because of impatience. It's not so much the tire rubber that's the problem, but the steel belt. With the reamer, you can't make the hole too big. It takes a while to wear the wire out. The rubber won't actually have as large a hole through it as the wire. It's possible to use a same-sized drill bit to do the same job, but I was too lazy to look for one. Apply the rubber cement liberally, because it's the only lubricant you have. After all that, the directions are detailed enough. I'll know in a couple of weeks if it held. So far it's not leaking. A better option is to take the tire to a shop and let them fix it, but it'll cost more. I've seen plugs that held up for the life of the tire tread. I know this one will, because I'll only use it if I have a flat on another tire.

title: Excellent carrier with a few simple modifications
text: Used immediately for a 2K mile trip and am very pleased with this cargo carrier. As recommended by other reviews, we did add the hitch extender to keep the carrier above the tailpipe to prevent melting of the plastic brackets (and the carrier rides very low) and we added locking hitch pins. We purchased a large cargo box from Home Depot that fit well with a few inches on either side and put ratchet tie downs on to secure and stabilize box to carrier. We bought a cargo box that had spaces on the top for a lock for extra security. We also added stick on reflectors to the carrier and box to alert drivers for extra safety. It looked so nice that we had people walk up to us at rest stops and ask about the cargo carrier. This is also very light weight and can be installed and handled by one person. So far the only concern is the longevity of the hitch extender as it is dependent on good welds but we check everything regularly at rests stops which is something you should do anyway regardless of the size of your load. One thing you might consider is how your trunk or hatch opens and whether it will interfere with your cargo. We have a Subaru Forester and the hatch just clears the top of the cargo box. So measure all hitches, distances, carrier and cargo/boxes if you anticipate having to access trunk/hatch while traveling.

title: Fast service.
text:
Replaced front and back shocks on E450 Class C. I went on the Bilstein website before purchasing. Of note, when ordering for your Class C, there are shocks listed for short and long wheelbase vans/Class C for the E450. Make sure you order the correct shock absorber for your wheelbase.

Also, changing shocks on any E450 that has the front lower mounts welded to the body are not a walk in the park. The driver's side is the worst. My husband modified some tools to get this job done. He also had to grind the bottom washer from 12 to 3 o'clock so that it would not hit against the frame. The shocks have to be compressed before installing (used stainless wire). Once he did that, took a breather, and enlisted my help to reach top of shock (my hands are smaller) he finally got the DS shock on. The passenger side was easier because we had the install procedure down to a science. The rear shocks seemed like a piece of cake compared to the front. When he finished, he took the zip ties off the rubber protectors and slid them up and rezipped 'em because they were all squished up.

I am not a mechanic. I am just describing what I watched my husband do, so don't be critical of my "technical " wording.

title: We stick with optilube
text: This works great in all our dodge diesels from our 2005 jeep liberty crd to our 2013 vw jetta tdi to our 2013 and 2003 Dodge trucks, also our son's 2006 gmc duramax.  The winter formula takes more ounces per gallons of fuel than the summer, so it doesn't go as far but is what you want when temperatures plunge in the teens and below zero from December through March (This year we had to start in November because of weather).  The XPD formula does fine for above 30 and has other advantages, so we like to use it for April, May, October, November.  We save our winter formula leftover til the next year and it is always just as good, soon to be starting on xpd and still need to use up our summer formula when it gets warm enough but will probably go to XPD for spring, summer and fall.  We started on this 2 1/2 years ago when my husband's cousin (a diesel mechanic for 30 years) recommended this.

title: Warm, soft, comfortable, works well with goggles while snow machining
text: I wear a helmet and this doesn't fit under my helmet, so I wear the thin one.  My husband's helmet was too small and he has been riding snow machines without a helmet, just this warmskin balaclava, goggles and a beanie and he stays nice and warm with no complaints.  My son also wore one of these and stayed nice and warm and it was pretty cold snow machining (about 15 degrees & cloudy).  They were in the powder and got snow  covered on the outside, but it didn't soak in, they still stayed warm even after dark and didn't take them off til they got to the truck.  Very nice.  You could put them under a helmet if the helmet isn't too tight.  I wish my helmet wasn't so tight.  My husband and son want a helmet with some room in it and then could use these nice warm balaclava under the helmet.  My helmet with the thinner balaclava stays warm for me and I mainly wear my helmet for warmth and all the powder they keep throwing on me when they scream by on their machines.

title: Makes a difference in sound, power and 1-2 mpg on fuel economy on all 5 diesels
text: We have 5 diesel vehicles.  A 2013 Dodge 3500 (pulls alot of trailers), 2006 GMC duramax, 2005 Jeep Liberty CRD, 2013 Volkswagon Jetta TDI and a 2003 Dodge 2500 5.9.  We use alot of opti-lube.  We (my husband's fault) accidentally put summer opti-lube in our 2003 (at -15 degrees!) and it gelled up (bad news)!  But we changed the filters, put in diesel kleen, then the winter opti-lube and fixed it right up again. But make sure you use the winter opti-lube in winter or at least the XPD formula.  We feel all the vehicles get improved fuel mileage with using our optilube. title: For best results focus on prep
text:
I am rebuilding my brake calipers and I wanted them to look nice when I was finished, so I purchased this paint and decided to give it a try.

I thought that I would test the paint first, so, I tested the paint on a two sample pieces of cast material. I know from a little bit of experience that if you want a good finish it requires a great deal of compatibility in prep. In other words make sure that your cleaning product is compatible with the paint.

The first thing that I did was cleaned the sample pieces, one I cleaned with brake cleaner and other cleaning products, the other test piece was cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner.

The first test piece that was cleaned with the brake cleaner and other cleaners, well, it didn’t turn out that great. The test piece appeared to be clean but for some reason or another the paint didn’t hold up as well as expected.

The second test piece that was cleaned in the ultrasonic cleaner was definitely the win. The paint went on smoothly and the end result was great.

I recommend that you use nitrile gloves throughout the entire process and never touch the cleaned surface of the item you are going to paint to avoid the transfer of oils from your skin to the item you are painting

title: WD-40 white lithium grease worked great on my garage door's lifting track
text:
I ordered this product because white lithium grease is required to grease down the center lifting mechanism for my garage door. The white lithium grease I've been using has been difficult to use since I walk with a cane so it is difficult to get on my short ladder to reach the coils (the roller rails on the sides use a different type of grease that comes in a spray can so I regularly spray them down as part of my system's preventive maintenance. That is probably why my garage door opener has lasted much longer according to the person who did my preventive maintenance last year. It is also very messy since I squirt some of the grease onto one part of the coils then I have to rub it to reach coils around it. Then I have to move my ladder down to repeat the process on a different area of the lifting coils.

When I had a garage door opener checkup a couple of months ago, I asked if he could grease the center lift. I was surprised to see that he came back from his truck with a can. When I asked him about it since I knew that only lithium grease could be used on the lifting mechanism, I asked him about it and she showed me that it was indeed a white lithium spray. When I saw him easily spraying the coils without having to stand on a ladder, I knew I had to buy lithium grease in a can!

Recently I've been having problems with my garage door opener. When I try to open my garage door from the wall unit, I have to hold down the button until the garage door reaches a certain height even though I knew that it was bad on the unit to do so. When I open my garage door using my remote unit, it is a taxing experience. When I would push and hold that button, the garage door would only go up a few inches and stop. When I pushed on the unit again, the garage door would go down. I would go through this process for at least 5 minutes. The colder it was, the longer it would take to open my garage door.

I knew that I needed to buy white lithium grease in a spray can. One would think that I would immediately think of ordering it from Amazon since I am a Prime member and order frequently but for some reason, I didn't. But I finally checked it out. I ordered WD-40 white lithium grease, first become of the good name recognition of WD-40. Then I checked out the Amazon reviews. Because it comes in a pressurized spray can, WD-40 white lithium grease has to be sent by ground transportation so no 2-day arrival with Prime. But my WD-40 white lithium grease arrived in four days - a day earlier than they had anticipated.

The next morning I used it. After opening the garage door the old way, I drove my truck out then I put the garage door down so I could reach the coils. I sprayed down my garage door's lifting track. When I got home from work that evening, I took a deep breath and pushed my garage door opener. Imagine my relief when my garage door has opened easily with just one short push! It has opened easily since I first sprayed it down. I'm glad that I ordered four cans to begin with. It will definitely be used as part of my garage door opener's preventive maintenance!

I was able to just strip the insulation and attached them to the taillight plug connectors. Zip tied and taped everything up and it works great. Since the switch is still attached I can turn it off/on and change settings if needed (although everything is tucked up under the rear fender - it's still easy to reach). Strobes are now activated whenever I turn on the headlights. Only issue is that the switch is exposed to any dirt/mud etc that the rear tires may kick up. So to protect that I plan on cutting the corner off a ziplock plastic bag and securing that over the switch, once I get some more zip ties (I ran out of them securing the cable to the ROPS). P.S. I read that someone completely bypassed the switch on a hardwire install and the strobe just cycles thru all the modes continuously - that might be fine too but have not tried this so I can't verify.

title: for an 08 Tahoe LTZ...
text:
(Sorry this review is so long; Cliff Notes:
THE SEAT COVER IS AESTHETICALLY PLEASING. THE SEAT COVER ITSELF IS GONNA BE LONG LASTING AND DURABLE. THE STRAPS HAVE TOO MUCH GIVE. THE COVER ISNT TOTALLY UNIVERSAL BUT PRETTY DARN CLOSE. Finally, I worry too much about what people think so I give toooooo many details. Those follow.)

... I note that my vehicle is an LTZ because it might be relevant to know that the [captain's chair style] passenger seat for which I purchased this cover has *all* the stuff underneath it: wires, more wires, then some more wires still, not to mention the front ways, up ways, back ways, down ways, seemingly even sideways mounts to support all those adjustment options that are powered by all those wires.

That explained, The sorta Celtic-looking discs did push through the back, between the seat bottom and the seat back sections, with just enough ease to keep them placed. They are rubber coated metal, btw, not plastic. The front hooks were too small to attach/latch onto the bar under the front of the seat bottom, so it took a little creative thinking as to how to make them stay. The elastic used for the 'stay straps' has too much give, in my opinion, which means it'll be perma-stretched (aka 'shot out') long before the seat cover itself. Deduct half a star for that, because I will be able myself to replace that elastic strap and see a new, more heavy duty one on when the perma-stretching occurs.

I deducted another half star for the straps that go under either side of the seat, hooking the sides down under the seat. Because my vehicle model has all those mounts underneath, there is (so far) no way to use those straps. When the humidity here isn't 'unbreathable air' and the heat isn't 'Hades with the heater on' and the pop-up-out-of-nowhere monsoons end (Summer in Georgia, 2022) I'll be able to reassess and figure out how to Redneck Rig those side straps to totally secure the seat cover from all sides.

My co-pilot is 99% of the time my 25 y/o Autistic, cognitively disabled, medically fragile son. His plethora of neurological diagnosis make him a squatter. No kidding, at least 50 times during a car ride I have to tell him "get your feet out of the seat" or "put your feet down". The only way to describe his posturing is the way you see an Australian Aboriginal squat. This has, over the 14 years I've owned my Tahoe, nearly ruined my seat. (I put him beside me, rather than the backseat, so if he seizes while I'm driving I can grab him if I need to while I pull over, to keep him from busting his head against the glass of his door window. I don't have a middle seat in the second row.)

title: When DIYing a window for the first time...
text:
...make sure you order enough to make mistakes. Lots of mistakes. I've used the static films before (11 windows, 2 half-glass exterior doors and a set of sliding glass doors) and that stuff is so simple and so easy and so durable. Walking too fast from your flat surface to your window and the static film will give with the breeze and not crease or bend or get damaged (for example... I'm a speedwalker with way too little patience to ever slow down 😫). I had 1 small bathroom window that gets full sun in the summer from 1pm until sunset. In Georgia. That little window will get you sunburned if ya gotta go 'see a man about a horse' at 3pm is all I'm saying 😅). The one roll of film was more than enough to do the top and bottom of the window and allow for one mistake. Welp, I made 2 mistakes because - again - zero patience and for some reason I was cutting wrong, as well. So I've ordered another roll to get it done. Still, less than $35 for 2 rolls and the lesson on window tinting. A pro would have cost me way way WAY more.

FWIW: I used a credit card with a piece of thin, soft washcloth folded over the edge as my squeegee and I made the application solution recipe Gila gives: 1 quart water to 1/2 capful of baby shampoo [I estimated half cap full to be 3 pumps from my big bottle of Equate Lavender Baby Bath). The instructions on the Gila website are the best; I'm all about YouTube tutorials but I preferred the Gila ones themselves. Sometimes 'tubers just talk too much and I lose what modicum of patience I have. Or my ADHD kicks in and I get lost - lol.

title: Nice Grip and Looks Cool
text:
One item that I now consider a necessity in any vehicle I drive is a steering wheel cover. They make gripping the wheel easier and they often add a touch of flair/style to an otherwise boring part of a car or truck’s interior. My current steering wheel cover was worn out and faded, so I decided to replace with this Sports Plaid Car Steering Wheel Cover, from ZATOOTO.

Like most steering wheel covers, this one is ready to go- just remove from the plastic wrap and start stretching it around your steering wheel. I usually start at the top, then work my way down. In a matter of less than a minute, the cover is in place and ready to use.

This steering wheel cover is a little thinner than my previous one, but it grips well, and gripping is the most important reason to add a steering wheel cover. Also, compared to my bare steering wheel, a cover like this means the steering wheel is less likely to feel extremely warm or cold, depending on the season. The feel on your skin is just right.

I like the added red stitching on this steering wheel cover. It adds a nice, albeit small, amount of contrast to the black color. You should try to place the red stitching at the top when you install. This is how it is intended and it looks better that way.

Steering wheel covers are a must. This ZATOOTO steering wheel cover is a cool way to make your steering wheel look and feel better. It’s priced right, too, and thus makes an excellent economical addition to your vehicle.

title: Quick Means to Revive Your Car Battery
text:
You never know when you may need help jump starting your vehicle. You could walk around and ask someone to help, You could call someone to come and help you jump your car. Or, you could reach for a portable jump starter like this one from BRPOM.

Out of the box, this jump starter is smaller than I expected. It comes nicely packaged and the owner’s manual tells you exactly how to use it. It is about 75 percent charged when you open the package, so it is ready to go immediately. I like the handy package because it keeps everything stored and ready to use, when you need it.

I must admit that I haven’t yet been able to test this jump starter to see how effective it is because- knock on wood- my battery hasn’t needed it, at least not yet. But I have been able to use this for other purposes, like for charging devices. I have placed it in my back seat and my kids can plug in their cell phones as needed to get a quick boost.

There is a flashlight on this device, but it isn’t very bright so I think I will keep a regular flashlight with me, in my car, in case an actual jump is needed. Until that time, I can only comment on the other features of this portable jump starter and from what I can see and what I have already used and tested, it seems like a good way to gain some added peace of mind.

title: Blocks out the Heat
text:
I live in south Texas where it’s hot and sunny most of the year. The blazing sun can lead to extreme temperatures inside your vehicle and it can take time for the AC to cool it down. Your interior can suffer damage, too. It’s best to fight back against the harsh rays of the sun and a way to do that is with this Yibaodan Car Windshield Sun Shade.

This windshield shade is a little different from others in that it’s umbrella style. You open it just like you would an umbrella, lock the latch in place, and press it against the inside windshield. There is an open section that fits around your rear- view mirror. It has a Velcro strap to help hold it in place, on your mirror. This also helps hold the umbrella itself in place and keeps the shade from falling.

I have had a good deal of success so far with this umbrella shade. I like that I can fold it up quickly, since it is like an umbrella, and I can store it under the seat or in the pocket on my driver’s side door. It does come with a leather case, but I have found it takes too much effort to wind it up tightly enough to fit inside the included case. Instead, I just treat it like an umbrella and stick in under the seat.

The handle of the umbrella doesn’t really have any place to rest when the shade is in use. I have found I have to rely on the Velcro, rear- view mirror holder to keep it secure. It would be better if there was something on my dash that I could prop the handle on, but there isn’t. And for this reason, it sags ever so slightly. As a result, the top edge of my wind shield isn’t covered and some sun does shine through. Still, this is a minor problem. The bulk of the sun is still blocked and my car is noticeably cooler than before.

Sunlight can get intense in Texas. Vehicle owners need something to block the hot and sometimes damaging rays and this umbrella is good for this purpose. The sagging concern prevents it from covering one- hundred percent of my windshield, but the coverage it does provide is adequate and it does make my car noticeably cooler inside.

title: Looks and Feels Great

title: Helps Organize My Hatchback
text:
My trunk is loaded with stuff common to most vehicles. I have a scraper, tire pump, grocery bags, a binder for work, and a few other things. I normally just let these items sit in my hatchback but I finally decided one day that my car would look much neater and cleaner if everything was placed in a storage bin of some sort and this need convinced me to get the CROROD Car Trunk Organizer.

With this organizer, you get a foldable, rectangular shaped storage bin with two removable dividers on the inside and a velcro seal. The unit isn’t very large- only about 20 inches long, 12 inches high, and 12 inches deep. This means it could be too small for a large vehicle with lots of stuff to store, but it works just right for my compact vehicle and its hatchback.

I am able to store my items in this organizer with no problem. I don’t need the two dividers, as I prefer the full space on the inside so that I can store items that are long and need more room. So, what I do is place a divider on each end of the inside, flat against each wall. This adds to the sturdiness of the organizer.

This storage organizer has a flap on top so that you can close it and keep your items hidden from view. If you have a fully closed trunk, this feature may not matter, but it does make a difference to me since I have a hatchback and anyone who walks past my car can see what is in the back with little effort. What I like about the flap is that it is bent on the long end, so that it closes and seals the organizer completely. This bent part is narrow and contains a strip of velcro. You don’t have to press it down. The angled flap drops into place and the velcro attaches itself with little or no effort on your part.

Trunks often need a little more organization and the CROROD Car Trunk Organizer is a good aid for the task. It could prove too small for some vehicles, but it works quite well in my small, compact car and satisfies my limited needs.

title: Good for Bicycle and Vehicle Tires
text:
Some tools are necessary for everyday living. Others are needed less frequently, but still highly important when the need arises. Air compressors fit into the latter category- you don’t need them much, but you will need them eventually. And Ring RAC630 Automatic Digital Compressor is a good compressor for several tasks.

I don’t have too many issues with my vehicle tires, but I do like to check the pressure periodically and re- inflate when necessary. A compressor like this is good for that purpose and the digital readout removes any guesswork. Manual tire pressure gauges require less effort to use, but you often cannot tell for sure what the pressure is. With the digital readout on this compressor, you feel more confident that the reading is accurate.

This compressor is a good thing to have around and I keep it stored in my car so it’s there when I need it. But the main reason I decided to get this compressor wasn’t for inflating car tires- it was for inflating bicycle tires. My kids ride their bikes frequently and the tires slowly lose air every few days. There never seems to be enough time to get the tires repaired/replaced to solve this problem. Instead, we just reach for a bike tire pump and inflate before each use. I have a manual pump that I could use, but I like this compressor better. I can see the pressure readout and feel better that the tire is inflated properly. And bicycle tires are so small, a compressor like this will inflate them in a matter of seconds. Yes, it is less convenient than a manual pump, but the accuracy is worth it.

Looking at other positives, the 10 foot cord is good because it is long enough to reach the different tires on most vehicles. The safety light is useful, too, and can come in very handy when you find yourself stranded at night with an underinflated tire. I also like that the adapters can be stored right here, with the compressor, so you don’t lose them. But one problem I have with this compressor is that it is somewhat lacking when it comes to intuitive design. There are buttons that perform various functions, but you cannot tell what they are for unless you experiment, which is not something many people are willing to do when they inflate a tire, basketball, etc. You will figure it out eventually, but the instructions could be better.

Flat tires and underinflated basketballs, soccer balls, and so on are an inevitable fact of life. We all need an air source and the Ring RAC630 Automatic Digital Compressor is a good tool for the job. It inflates most anything in a short time with digital readout so you can feel confident that the pressure is accurate. A good compressor overall with just a few minor issues, so certainly something I recommend.

title: Accutire MS- 5550 Works, but has its Issues
text:
Ready to use out of the box and reasonably lightweight, the Accutire MS-5550 is a fairly versatile tool for inflating everything from car tires to basketballs. It comes with multiple attachments that make it useful for inflating these different devices and with the capability of 300 psi, it can inflate most anything that needs pumped up.

Like most households, mine needs an air compressor from time to time, especially for inflating bicycle tires, which just never seem to hold their air. This air compressor works okay for occasional use and I like that it utilizes a digital readout gauge for easier readings and offers an emergency light for nighttime use. The device comes with a two year warranty and with the included attachments, I have used it to inflate basketballs and other sporting devices. Based on these facts, Accutire MS-5550 seems like a sure winner and a good air compressor for the average household.

However, once you have used this air compressor a few times, you quickly recognize some of its shortfalls. The first annoyance is with the air line- it has a difficult time clamping itself tightly on the stem of a bicycle tire or regular tire. If the stems are long enough, you may have better luck but otherwise, there is a good chance it will not form a tight seal and that means each time you try to turn on the power and start pumping, it will shut off after a few seconds. It does this with my bicycle tires and vehicle tires. I have to pump these items up gradually, a few spurts of air at a time. The device does work better with basketballs, volleyballs, etc. Since you need to use a needle- type attachment for these types of things, there is no need to worry about the seal and thus it has no problem inflating to the desired level and then shutting itself off.

One other quality I wish was different is the power cord. All you get is a car cord, and that means you will need a vehicle nearby in order to use the compressor. It really needs another cord- one that plugs into an ordinary household outlet. If you use it on bicycles or basketballs like I do, you have to plug it into a car or truck. There is no other option, making it less convenient.

So, in a nutshell, Accutire MS-5550 is an acceptable air compressor for certain uses, but not for others. It is best at inflating small objects, so- so for bicycle tires, and not so good with vehicle tires because it continuously shuts off and adds the psi's at a lethargic rate. Chalk this one up as an average device overall that may or may not suit individual needs.

title: Have You Checked Your Tire Pressure Lately?
text:
Checking tire pressure should be a routine task, to ensure proper inflation, improve tire life, add extra miles per gallon, etc. Few people bother to check their tire pressure on a routine basis, but the Accutire MS-4350B Programmable Digital Tire Gauge strives to make this task as simple and painless as possible. This tire gauge offers digital accuracy, placing it a notch above most mechanical pressure gauges. The display numbers are large and incremented in 0.5 psi. This provides an accurate readout, better ensuring that tires are properly inflated.

To use this gauge, all you need to do is press the tip of the gauge into the stem and then wait for the sound of a beep. If you do not hear a beep, then you do not have a sealed connection and you cannot rely on the accuracy of the psi readout. This would seem simple enough and it generally is, but I have had a few issues with this. On my minivan, the stems are shorter and are somewhat recessed between the grooves in the wheels. This makes it more difficult to establish a connection and get an accurate reading. Sometimes, I cannot achieve the seal, never hear the beep, and end up deflating some air from my tires in the process as I continue to try without any luck.

One other possible issue with this gauge is that the pressure readout doesn't stay on the screen for very long. Once the beep has sounded, the pressure is displayed and you have only a matter of seconds to remove the gauge and read the pressure. If you don't act quickly, the panel will go blank. I don't know why the manufacturer made it this way. If it would last at least ten seconds, it would make a big difference.

The programmable buttons for front and rear tire pressure are basically a novelty item with this gauge. They allow you to set a target psi level for the front and back tires, and this could be helpful in some instances. The reason I say this is a novelty is because it serves as nothing more than a reference point. The gauge won't warn you if your pressure is too high or too low. The preset amounts are only there for your reference. Also, there is only a single set of preset numbers so if you have multiple vehicles, you will have to decide which one to set.

Checking tire pressure is important and the Accutire MS-4350B Programmable Digital Tire Gauge is a good way to check pressure periodically. It offers an easy to read, blue LCD readout and a small light to help check pressure in dark spaces. You may have problems making a connection if your tire stems are recessed in any way, but other than that, you should have no trouble using this Accutire gauge. Just a quick press lets you know if your tire pressure needs to be adjusted, leading to better gas mileage for your vehicle and longer- lasting tires.

title: Compact and Handy Device from Black & Decker
text:
Air compressors are helpful devices and Black and Decker manufactures a few for consumer use. This model is compact in size, cordless, and generally convenient thanks to its ability to inflate everything from car tires to air mattresses and more.

One thing I noticed immediately with this air compressor is that its operation is not as intuitive as I would like. When I first received this device, I removed it from the box and proceeded to test it out by checking and partially inflating my car tires. To my surprise, it didn't work. I then opened up the owner's manual and learned that the unit will not work this way. You have to preset the desired tire pressure first or else the high pressure inflator side of the device will not function. And to set the desired pressure, well, again, you need to read the owner's manual because it requires pressing two buttons at once until you find the desired pressure measurement, then holding the buttons until the numbers flash, then pressing the plus or minus key until you reach the desired pressure. Intuition isn't built- in, so don't bother trying to figure this out on your own- reading the owner's manual is the way to go.

Other slight problems exist with this Black & Decker air compressor, among them the problems with achieving a seal and the short hoses. The most important problem is that the high- pressure inflator will not work if you cannot achieve the proper seal. The reason is because the locking arm, at the tip of the hose, has to be firmly sealed or else the unit will not function properly. I had this happen with my first few attempts to use this on my tires and I couldn't understand what was wrong. I soon discovered that if the tip of the hose is not fastened securely and sealed completely, the unit will not work and will react in a strange way. It will start to pump air for a few seconds, then shutoff, then display the maximum pressure on the LCD readout, then slowly fall. The first time this happened, I thought something was seriously wrong with my tires. But then, I removed the hose and checked the pressure with a separate gauge one more time and it was normal. I then learned that this problem is caused by not having the hose locked firmly in place. Depending on the construction of your tires, wheel covers, etc., you may not be able to secure the seal and hence will not be able to use this device. I also have an issue with the short hoses. Both of the included hoses are very short and thus the unit has to be placed very close to the item in need of inflation. Another small criticism is the noise level. For something this small, it certainly is capable of making itself known and it can get annoying very quickly from close range.

Looking at the good points, I like that this air compressor offers both high pressure and high volume inflation options with a separate hose for each. I also like the multiple accessories included with this air compressor and I like that each of the two hoses and the car cord can be wrapped around the unit and locked into place. This makes for a less than attractive appearance, with all of those hoses and cord in view, but it is convenient to be able to wrap everything up right on the outside of the unit. And, of course, the compact size is quite nice. It is small enough to hide away in several places in your vehicle or elsewhere, completely out of sight.

So, judging this Black & Decker air compressor overall, I must say that it's a handy device for inflating tires, air mattresses, and other items. If you buy it with the primary intention of using it on your vehicles tires, be aware that unless you have enough clearance, you may not be able to achieve the proper seal on the tire stem and therefore will be unable to use the unit. But other than this and a few minor cosmetic issues, this Black & Decker air station is a handy little compressor, with multi- inflation capabilities and multiple accessories to accommodate your various needs.

title: All I need is the shaft and I have to pay $50 for this entire kit
text:
I've broken more impellers on products like these than I'd like to count. In the HOB line you will pay $40 just for an impeller on a $50 Filter RIP OFF. So for the HOB's I just buy an entire new filter. This isn't quite so bad - the maintenance kit that's way more stuff than we need and is only about 1/4th the price of the $219 filter. And we don't even know if this will fix it.

The thing is though, we only need the ceramic impeller stick. All the rest we'll just keep in a plastic bag and when I die in a few years, and they sell the rest of this in an estate sale everybody will wonder what it was for - by then we will likely have broken even more impeller shafts. Just 5 cents of highly engineered ceramic which, frankly, is a STUPID material to make this out of. Now if I could pay $1 and just buy the shaft, I'd be the happiest customer in the world. But right now, I'm not feeling too good about it/ Bought the filter last June and finally got the "custom" tank it was for 6 months later
. Put it in for a month and it breaks. And we don't even know if this will fix it. Originally all we were going to do was put some silicone sealants and plumbers' tape around the gasket hoping that would stop the top of this filter from leaking. I asked my assistant to do that because 90% of the videos I spent a day watching determined the casket needed to form a tighter seal and they used rubber band + gasket, Silicone or vegetable oil + gasket every few months and no more leaks and it didn't cost $50 so we take it apart prepared for the silicone treatment and he pulls on the impeller which immediately either broke or was already broken. In the meantime, I've been treating a 90-gallon tank with Armguard because I have a foot-long DoJoe loach that puts out enough ammonia to pollute Kansas, so we bought him what I thought was the best canister filter on the planet. We used it a month or two - then it starts leaking all over my beautiful hardwood floors . This better fix the problem. UPDATE: 2/22/22: added the new impeller shaft re-greased and re-seated the gasket and the thing still leaks in one corner. Bought the filter prematurely in April 2021 - then there was a several months delay on the construction and delivery of my 90 gallon tank (which I hate - no more acrylic - actually no more tanks, I'm done. ) So we start messing with the filter in June of 2021 until we saw cracks in the top of the 90 gallon tank - sent that back and got a new one (Clearview - pain in the bu** due to the lack of openings on the top for hoses, heater lines etc. But tried the filter once more. It immediately leaked. Resealled the gasket and it still leaks, noticed the impeller shaft was broken (it is ceramic and fragile - and no doubt keeps things quiet but even metal impeller shafts break easy - don't use ceramic. Put it all together today - and it leaks, in exactly the same place as it's always leaked- down one corner of the filer. Same corner since the first time we used it, Hope Fluval has a 1 yr warranty so I can get a new one or get my money back ($219 for the filter and another $50 for a head kit when we just needed an impeller shaft AND IT STILL LEAKS.) I swear I'm done with fishkeeping if I can't get a working filter from them. It is a MONEY PITT of a hobby and just when I've started my salt water tank - which is a money pit on steroids. What was I thinking when I started this "hobby" 4 yrs ago after my husband died?. Hobbies are supposed to be fun, relaxing, even challenging is fine but I've had nothing but manufacturing errors on nearly every filter I've purchashed (mostly HOB's) I have a huge box of spare parts because only an impeller shaft broke and I had to (like this one) buy a kit - which in the case of the HOB's cost only $10 less than a whole new filter. Now this company makes impeller shafts out of ceramic - when even the metal are sure to break and so they use an even easier to break shaft? And in the end it didn't matter, it still leaks.

title: You will be amazed
text: My 2008 Subaru with Newport blue paint was extremely oxidized and was very dull, almost chalky looking. I started with a good wash followed by going over every inch with a clay bar. I used the orange pad and V32 compound to polish with. Even after extensively cleaning the car, the orange polish pad almost seem to get loaded up with removing the oxidation after only doing half of the vehicle. The pad did last long enough to finish the entire job but was starting to disintegrate on the last quarter panel. I am amazed at how good the paint looks now. All of the chalky finish is completely gone! The car is shinier than I’ve ever seen it, even with just doing the one pass using the orange pad and V32. I’ve ordered additional orange pads and another bottle of the compound and plan on going over the entire car one more time before working my way up to the next, less abrasive compounds and pads. I’ve never been overly concerned with keeping my car clean, but using the 10FX tool and polishing kit was a lot of fun and I believe that I will be taking a lot better care of my vehicles from now on.

title: Love this kit, but buy extensions if you have a larger RV
text:
I love this system, though if you have a larger RV (mine's 52'), you'll want to buy extra long hoses up front. I'm new to RV'ing, so when I got a good deal on a used 52' 5th wheel I didn't understand how difficult my life would be. I didn't want to mess with stinky hoses so I bought this kit. The kit is good enough for most folks, but anything larger than say 30' (arbitrary, guessing), you'll want to buy extra long hoses to guarantee you can reach the connections.

I tried hard to find generic hoses in various hardware stores, but was unable to. Luckily a small-town RV store was able to rush me Valterra's proprietary hoses; more expensive that way, but otherwise guaranteed fitting. Take note, if you do buy extensions, pick up extra hose clamps, as they extension hoses don't come with enough (I wanted to make sure, so I added one everywhere a piece connected to another piece).

I can't recommend enough how much I like this kit. The only complaint I have (though it could be user error), is when my "fresh water" line is on (to force water into the tank or down the output line), I have a leak at the adapter. In the picture, it's at that green auto-coupler at the RV septic tank's output. It's not a severe leak, but it tends to spray w/high force upwards (mine kinda is aimed back towards the RV, so I don't get wet really).

title: Double check
text: Well this is more of a teaching moment than a product review. They normally don't leak right out of the box unless you get a defective one or worse.. always always always seal the threads with pipe tape or a thin film of gasket sealer (the high temp ones are usually better as the block gets extremely hot), never overtitghen them (the is the worse I started earlier) because you can stretch the threads or strip them out all together, make sure you put the sensor on straight (as not to cross thread it) what I do is start threading the sensor without any tape or seal to kind of clean the threads (if you have a thread chaser use that) and then back it out put on my high temp sealer on the threads and go as far as I can hand tightening it. Getting a torque wrench on it might be hard because of very little space so I use a torque wrench adapter that goes in between the sensor socket and ratchet. Before connecting the clip to the sensor make certain the pins are straight and also check the wiring  for breaks or damaged wires... I hope this helps at least a few people or it may not help anybody at all ... Nevertheless try and be patient, go slow, know your limits, use the right tools, and enjoy the fruits of your labor.. if anyone has any questions I am on Facebook Micheal Sharp.. please enjoy your day and God bless

title: Easy-to-use and reliable results
text:
At one time, a driver could get a quick checkup of the oil, windshield-wiper fluid, and tire pressure at a local full-service gas station. That kind of service is hard to find nowadays; to get tires checked, many of us now rely on service at a tire store that may be many miles away from home.

As a 70-year-old woman, I was a bit dubious about buying this tire pump and concerned that I might not understand the technical instructions for operating the pump. No worries. It is simple to use. It's best to read the instructions first so that you can visually imagine yourself using the pump. It is very similar to using a tire gauge except that you can use the up and down arrows on the pump to preset the pressure that you wish to achieve. After pressing the start button, you just wait for the pump to inflate the tire. With my small hatchback needing only 32.5 PSI or so, the pump took about two or three minutes per tire.

It turns itself off after reaching the preset PSI. I checked the PSI reading with a tire guage. All four tires were preset to 32.5 on the pump. The tire gauge read 31.4 - 31.7 per tire after using the pump. I thought perhaps the lower readings were due to lost pressure as I pressed the tire stems while removing the pump and adding the gauge.

I used the wall charger to complete the first full charge before use, as instructed.

The only "quirk" worth mentioning is that the pump must be charged fully, and the green light indicating a full charge is on the charger, not on the pump.

There are a few safety instructions depending on the size of the tire. It's best to read these thoroughly to be sure that you use the pump safely and also extend the life of the device and the battery.

After cleaning the car window with 97% isopropyl alcohol I had to go back several times with my credit card to add pressure and I also pulled from multiple angles to get the backing off. Take your time. Don't rush and it'll work. You're not done! Now you need to press the vinyl down onto the car window. Once you get that done you peel the clear fronting plastic off making sure the decal stays where you wanted and. . . done. Now we just have to see how it weathers and handles car washes over time. I don't have a lot of decorations on my car but I really liked this design. It looks great.
Edit: I was just looking at the picture I took for this review and realized that the hand giving the bird is a left hand. Being a lefty myself this made the sticker all the more special to me.

Update - It's March 30th 2021, I applied this is 2019. Looks as sharp as the day it went on. Has gone through numerous car washes and driven through many a Florida storm.

title: Saved Me a Trip to the Dealership
text: Literally the day after I got this scanner I was out driving around a wildlife refuge taking pictures. The road had some horrible potholes. Apparently some gas must have sloshed into the vapor return system and charcoal canister tripping off a check engine light. I'm 30 miles from home, there's no one to come get me if it's serious. A tow would be a fortune. . . Then I realized that I had tossed the OBD2 scanner in the backseat just to have along. I popped the cover and plugged it in expecting the worst news (that's how my life goes) and I found the cause was a common evap error the bad roads and a full tank just mixed enough to trip the warning. I cleared the CEL and drove back roads home but the light stayed out so it was just happenstance. The scanner allowed me to see the check engine light was just a nothing thing and not the engine about to self destruct. Saved me whatever insane hourly rate and scan fees the dealership would have hit me with. This is staying with my car from now on!

text:

The filter itself appears to be a quality build. The dark coloration from the activated carbon is, at first, disconcerting and may make future inspection difficult.
