title: Install not too bad
text:
Installed on a 2011 Chevrolet Silverado 2500HD with the 6.0 gasoline motor. The rear drivers side exhaust bolt had broken off, like ALL of the Silverado trucks do. The exhaust leak was more of a nuisance really, knowing I have a $40K truck with cheap Chinese bolts that break themselves because of low carbon content. Every time I started it up in the mornings, that annoying exhaust leak! Thank you GM for purchasing cheap chinese junk metal bolts!!
This bracket fixed that annoying little leak. Took about 45 minutes to install.
The very first thing you will want to do, is on the firewall, right behind the engine, is a small heat shield held on by 3 10mm nuts. One at the top of the shield, and two at the bottom down by the floor board. Remove those 3 nuts first, and slide the heat shield down and just lay it on the exhaust for the bracket install.
For the removal of the grounding strap bolt (If yours is so equipped), a 15mm ratchet wrench is needed.
Remove the short grounding strap bolt from the rear of the engine.
Ensure you use anti-sieze on the bolts for the bracket install. You will need a 14mm ratchet wrench for install.
I put the bolts through the grounding strap and the bracket, slid the bracket behind the engine, and hand tightened the two bolts. The ratchet wrench makes short work of this, and the bottom bolt is much easier to reach from under the truck. Once those are tightened down, install the clamp bolt, and ensure you use high temp, high strength loc-tite when installing this. The last thing you want to have to do, is find another bolt to replace this one if it vibrates out.
Tightening this bolt down was easiest using a 1/2" ratchet, 14mm socket, swivel, and 4" extension. The firewall is in the way on the drivers side, and you cannot really use a socket without the swivel and extension. And the ratchet wrench will not fit, due to the bracket.
Tighten everything down, and then reinstall the small heat shield. Allow the loc-tite to cure, and then test it out.
It works like a champ on my truck. No more noisy exhaust leak!!
Highly recommended!!

Installed on a 2009 Silverado 1500. Installation is not as easy as most of the videos would suggest. Especially if you are installing on an older truck.
I have plenty of experience working on vehicles, as well as the proper tools. If you do not have the proper tools, this job will take you quite some time.
You will need to separate the upper A arm from the knuckle assembly and remove your drag link. Make sure you have a 6 ton bottle jack as well. You will need this to push your knuckle assembly back up to reconnect the upper A arm.
Took my son and I about 2.5 hours per side. This was due to rusted and stuck bolts and hardware.
The spacer itself, is exactly as described, and it works as it should. Nothing bad to be said about the spacer. Just be aware of the level of experience when taking on this job.

title: Supposed to be OEM fit
text: These shocks are approximately 1" shorter than OEM shocks. This may not seem like much, however, when you tear down the old strut assembly and try to put them together, that 1" may as well be one mile. We could not get the springs compressed down enough to get these shocks in and reassembled. And that was using the proper spring compression tool. And even if you could get it compressed enough to re-assemble, the strut assembly would be 1" shorter. A huge deal if you are trying to level your truck with a leveling kit. Plus, the strut shaft is a larger diameter than the OEM. The bump stop inside the strut assembly will not fit on the shaft. So IMHO, the best thing to do, is to purchase a complete assembly and swap out the whole assembly.

title: Dont waste your time or money.....
text:
This "seems" like a great idea....however, if you have owned a camper long enough, you come to realize that the majority of the canopy failures is right at the point where the canopy attaches to the camper. The failure point on most canopies is that it rips along the round nylon attaching material. This cover does not protect that point of the awning. When you clip this on, it only covers the awning that is exposed when in the stored position. So basically it only covers about 8 -10 " of fabric. The awning will still be full of water after a rainstorm, because the water runs along the awning tube and inside the awning. The ONLY way an awning cover would protect your awning in the way this advertises to, would be to have a cover that will enclose the entire tube and awning assembly. A zip up vinyl "Bag" of sorts. This plastic cover is just a gimmick.
The best way I have found to maintain your awning, is to regularly clean it, open it up after a rain storm to allow it do dry out, and apply a good vinyl protectant.

They have been on the truck for a couple of months now, and it is my daily driver. No moisture in the lights, and no other problems so far.

title: Excellent Product
text:
I was skeptical in spite of all the positive reviews, but Mechanic in a Bottle absolutely solved my problem.
I heartily recommend MIB for any of the symptoms it's advertised to cure.
Here's my story:

I ran my two year old 4-cycle gas mower out of gas while cutting the lawn. I refilled the tank, but the mower refused to run for more that a few seconds. I suspected old fuel in spite of having used Sta-Bil, so I drained the tank and refilled with freshly bought gas. Same symptoms. Then I reckoned that some particles of sludge from the bottom of the tank may have made it to the carburetor when I ran it dry.

I went looking for a product to dissolve it. I've used various carb cleaners and gas additives in the past. Those that actually worked also were dangerous to plastic parts. I read about MIB and got some at my local hardware store.
I followed the MIB directions of 2 oz in an empty tank for a non-starting engine (as opposed to a rough running one). I primed the engine by pulling the cord three times with the spark plug disconnected (no primer bulb on my mower). Then I let it sit over night. The next day I added a half tank of gas and pulled. The motor started immediately and died in a few seconds. Not unexpected with pure MIB in the Carb. I pulled again. The engine started again and smoothed out after about 15 seconds of running rough. It continued to run very smoothly. I hadn't realized that my engine had previously been running rough until I experience its post-MIB performance.

MIB solved my problem without a doubt. I love the like-new way the mower runs now. I will be using MIB as a regular additive from now on.

title: Identical to BMW branded part.  Comes with control & bulbs
text:
Hella is the OEM to BMW for this headlamp assembly, and I found the H1141001 identical to the factory assembly. The one I ordered from Amazon came with all the lamps and the control module (ballast).

When researching this Hella part number I checked various suppliers offering the part to see if the lamps and control were included. Hella said yes, but several of the lower cost vendors I called told me the ballast and lamps were not included. It was not always clear from their ads as they all offered the H1141001 number. I suspect some of them removed and parted out the ballast and lamps separately.

That said, the control can be easily transferred from an old assembly and is not likely to have been damaged in a collision. Save money and reuse you old one if you can. The bulbs can be transferred as well if they are still good, but don't handle the glass parts as your fingers will leave oil deposits that carbonize under heat.

text: I purchased these mats from this seller specifically because I saw mats made by them in a 2021 Pacifica.  I have a 2019 Dodge Grand Caravan.  I loved how my friend's Pacifica mats came together with velcro and had really well defined edges to prevent spills from rolling off the edges.  When my mats arrived, they were in a large box and folded.  I purchased the set of 4 (one for each front seat; one for the middle row; and one for the back row) in black.  I would advise being careful when putting them in or move them around (you will have to almost completely remove the middle row for when you want to utilize stow-and-go) because the bottoms are made to "grip" the floor of the car and the fibers are hard and poke well.  I actually had one stuck in my hand when I installed them.  Pulled it out like a splinter.  These for the Dodge Caravan do not have velcro and do not meet too well between the middle and last row.  They do overlap some in areas.  On the left passenger side the seatbelt bolted to the floor for the middle row doesn't allow for the mat to lay down completely.  The mats would not lay down flat when I first got them at all.  It took several days for them to finally do so.  They are some very tight spots for the mats too up against the chairs.  You really have to push them down hard to make them "snap" into place so to speak.  The driver side and front passenger side mats fit really well but there are domes to cover where the manufacturers mats lock into place with a hook.  These mats I cannot get to cover the hook.  They are slightly off.  That bugs me.  I have wiped them down with a wet cloth several times so far to clean them.  They are not mats you can easily remove quickly and shake out and then wipe down.  They are stiff and again, that backing!  However, they wipe well enough off in place.  I have run a vacuum over them too and it left some marks.  I won't do that again.  I will use a brush head on the shop vac.  These mats are labeled with a tag showing Caravan model years through 2017.  I initially thought I had received the incorrect mats.  I reached out to the seller through Amazon and they assured me they were the correct mats and that no changes were made (or significant enough) between the model years 2017 and 2019 to change the design.  I had trouble receiving and sending info to the seller through Amazon.  Amazon would not allow me to upload any pictures to send to the seller.  I had to go out and search the seller online through Google to find a way to contact them via email.  They finally received my pictures through email.  They were responsive enough to me and my questions.  I am not completely happy with them and had I known there was no velcro and such tight fits I probably would have gone with another brand.  However, I am keeping these and they are covering well.  I like the look of them as well.  They are not rubbery and I am happy with that.  These pictures were taken just shortly after first installing them and were shared with the seller.  The circled areas are where bubbles were and the mats would not lay flat.  Those areas are now flattened.  So if yours is doing the same, give it some time.  The other pictures are of areas where the mat was tight to get into place.  Also, the dome to cover the hook for the original mat on the driver side is shown in a picture here.  I cannot get that dome to fit over the hook.

title: Very good product.  Keeps car batteries in better, long lasting conditions.
text:
Great unit to extend your car battery's life.

I have too many cars. Mostly BMWs. My wifes is a newer one (a 335i) with a lot of communication messages & check systems & complexity. The yellow battery warning light had come on several times on this car. This means: get ready to buy a new battery.

So I got this unit to help my cars that sit stationary & also to help me change out the battery in this 335i because the power cannot be interrupted when the battery is changed.

Before I swapped out the car's battery, I hooked up this Battery Minder. Now, you can't get a reading on the power level of batteries with this unit. After reading the manual, you get an understanding that this unit determines if the battery can be re-charged & if yes, it starts doing it's process. After an hour, the unit finished it's steps of re-charging & then went in to battery maintenance mode. So this product revitalized the battery. It's been 2 months since & there hasn't been any more yellow battery warning lights with the car. Very nice!

This product also does desulfating which really helps the battery life (I'm no scientist & never had heard of this before). Battery Tender does not do this & this is why I bought the Battery Minder instead. In fact, I had never heard of the Battery Minder brand. Only the Battery Tender I have seen on TV commercials. But based on my research, I chose the Battery Minder. I'm happy I did.

title: Update to the Update to the initial review
text:
[[VIDEOID:2aed7200a333d5acfb4ff203a8714e00]] Well we contacted Clear2O with our problem received an immediate response asking for video and to answer several questions. I provided the video and answered the questions, after a week I followed up with an email inquiring if they received the video. Well haven’t heard back from Clear2O and I don’t hold out much hope. We added this to our inline filter for camping. It has been great. No after taste, no sediment or ease use and clean up.

This worked great for two long weekend trips. Followed directions how to maintain the filter. On our third trip the filter begin leaking where the top and bottom meet. Absolutely nothing I tried to include putting plumbers tape on it stopped the leak. So if you only plan to use it twice excellent purchase if more DONT BUY.

After contacting Clear2O they sent a replacement filter and I sent the old one back. The problem was: there is a seal/gasket/washer between the lid and the body. The first one did-not have this seal. One answer is it was never there and until the third use it was ok. Second answer is during a cleaning session I inadvertently lost the seal. As anal as I am about equipment I think I would have kept this seal but there you go.

Now since receiving the replacement with the seal and making extra special Effort not to lose it.
The filter works great we at one location for two days and upon breaking everything down I noticed the inner filter had a red tint and there were some small rust particles in the filter. I am very pleased with the filters performance and would recommend it again. I have it four instead of five stars for the issue in the beginning.

I plan to buy a second one when I need it.

title: Buy the OEM parts
text: This is a review for both the left and right parking brake cables for a 2008 Tacoma.  The length was correct but overall the quality of manufacture was lower than the OEM ones I took off.  The clamp points are rubber "sliders" as opposed to the fixed metal ones on the original equipment.  On the passenger side, the heat shield is minimal in comparison to the original equipment.  Both of those things are minimal compared to the fitment of the cables into the tunnel under the cup holder.  The Toyota version has a rubber boot that is several inches long, which gives the installer some ability to seat it correctly from the elements.  This dorman one has a boot that is maybe an inch long and was difficult to work with.  I finally gave up.  My truck is 11 years old, so I'm not too worrried about it rusting out.  But if I had to do it all over again, I would buy the OEM parts.

title: Great product and built tough!  Know your tongue weight.
text:
Love the jack! Well packaged product and heavy duty design. Using it on a Keystone Sprinter 277rls (32’) travel trailer, 8000lb loaded, tongue weight of 800lbs. It was easy to install, easy to wire and simple to operate; one switch for up/down and other for lights. Actual install time was less than 30 minutes, but with prep time it took me about an hour (getting tool ready, taking stuff out of the box, tie wrapping wiring, shrink wrap connectors, getting rid of trash, etc.) Note: when you bolt the jack down, take time to make sure the star washers actually dig into the metal and not just the paint. This is your ground. I had to scratch a little paint off after it didn’t work the first time.
The version I bought came with breaker switch instead of a fuse which I like and all wiring was 10 gauge wiring so very sturdy. The trailer connector storage bracket was not on the back of the unit as shown in some pictures; it actually was separate from the jack and was the type you can connect around the tube under the motor or you can mount somewhere else also (see picture). I like that as I have propane tanks right behind my jack and I placed mine on the side under the motor.
The motor is fairly fast compared to other cheaper models and I don’t see any issue with speed especially since you have adjustments in the lower leg that can quickly get the jack stand closer to the ground. It is quiet for an electric motor but is a bit louder under pressure.
It is weather resistant but I would store it with some type of cover. I selected a cover made from sunbrella material which sheds rain but allows it to breath.
And in some comments there seems to be some confusion about weight capacity. For a tongue jack you need to know your max tongue weight of your trailer which should be in your owner's manual. You DO NOT need to buy a jack which can lift your whole trailer. (Trailer tongue weight is the downward pressure that the coupler places on the hitch ball.) Typical tongue weight is 10-15% of total weight so for example a 10,000lb max trailer will generally have a tongue weight of 1000-1500lbs. Also when computing jack capacity, plan a little extra if you are slightly lifting the back of your tow vehicle with the trailer tongue for weight distribution hookup/removal if you have that installed. Of course an electric jack adds a "little" weight to your tongue as well but not much. Choose a jack with a capacity that at least surpasses your max tongue weight. Having a jack that is rated for more than the tongue weight is not a problem but I find it hard to imagine anyone needing more than a 3000 lift for most any travel trailer application unless you have a very heavy trailer max weight (>20,000lbs) or you want bells and whistles not on this mode. This 3000lb lift is fantastic and almost 3x what I would ever require.

Also to connect breaker I used waterproof heat shrink ring connector (napa part # 785918) for the battery connection and butt connectors (napa part #784442) for wiring.

Update July 21, 2016: Been using this jack for several weeks and has been great. Very powerful, mostly quiet, very quick if you adjust the footing manually first, and has been a back and arm saver! Should have bought this a long time ago. It also stays out in the weather under a sunbrella cover and is working great. Had other campers buy other jacks half this price only to replace those only a year later and are very slow and loud. I would not hesitate buying this again but hope I don't have to.

title: Some adjustment needed
text:
These pads "fit" into the jack bracket of the named BMW vehicles. There is a need for a change in the molding of the rectangular top of the jack pad itself. The rectangle measures 2 millimeters TOO SHORT to bear the weight of the vehicle where it is supposed to be supported. The EDGES of the affixed jack bracket on the car is NOT meant to be a load bearing surface. It will crack. It is the center of the jack bracket which should carry the lifting load. The easy fix is to obtain a 2 millimeter thick piece of material which can be glued to the rectangular top of these pads. Then you will have the necessary load potential which will keep you from messing up either these jack pads or the jack brackets affixed to the vehicle.

Of further note. You should already have a rubber saddle bracket on your lifting jack. These pads just sit on top of that. When finished with your lift. You place these jack pads back into the compartment which looks like a drink glass holder in the trunk where the battery resides in most BMW's.

Not a ton, but a little.... so.... plan for that. Seal your contents inside tightly closed garbage, or contractor sized bags like we did. Problem solved.......This should be obvious anyway.

We don't have storage racks on top of either of our vehicles so these were seriously an answer to prayer. After the cross country moving trailer hauled most of our things away, we needed to stay behind with some left over gear to wrap things up. You'd be surprised how that little bit of stuff adds up!! title: Stuff to know
text:
This freezer/cooler has great cooling...works well thus far...24 hours. Problem is, it isn't really optimized for storage. I like the compressor on top. It claims 13.2 gallons or 50 liters...I can tell you, unless you just fill it with water, it won't hold 13.2 gallons. An example, if you used gallon milk jugs, you might fit 6 inside with some space around the edges for other stuff. Looks to me more like 10-11 gallons at best. Also, the cooler I got wasn't made by Cho sports. It was some company named Massimo. Anyway, so far for what it holds, it works.
edit: It has no interior light either...using A/C power, when compressor is on it uses between 48 and 82 watts (it goes up and down), when the compressor is off it uses 1.2 watts.
After a few days there is a slight frost layer on the interior walls, that layer was there after 24 hours and hasn't gotten thicker 2 days after that. Frost is often caused by opening and closing the door frequently.

edit: 07/29/2020 - Freezer still going strong on 24/7 in our place. We can't even hear the compressor unless we are next to it and everything else is off. So far, so good.

To deal with the lack of an internal light, we bought a pack of stick on motion sensing lights (they sell them on Amazon, of course). Now when we open the top, the light comes on. Just make sure to stick it high up on the cooler wall so it doesn't get in the way.

We'd much rather hook this up to our generator than a full size fridge during a power outage. Big savings on wattage.

edit: 10/10/2020 - yup...still working. No issues thus far.
edit 12/15/2020 - Still working great. 6 monthaversary.
edit: 05/22/2021 - Still going strong. 11 months 24 hours a day in our home on A/C power.
edit: 07/23/2021 - Working great...I've defrosted it 2x since buying it and the frost layer never got
more than about 1/8th of an inch and then only where the coils are located under the freezer walls.

title: Better than stock, but beam pattern not sharp (2012 Pathfinder)
text: HB5 / 9007 LED replacement in a 2012 Nissan Pathfinder. Installation was not quite plug and play. Once I figured out I had to disassemble the bulb to get the 9007 specific ring inserted into the housing first, the rest was easy. It came with zip ties because the ballast resistor made for a longer cable, that I zip tied to the harness so it would not flop around in the engine bay. No flicker or codes appeared so far, so I was happy with that. The light is clean and white, and brighter than the stock halogens, even a bit brighter than Sylvania Silverstars halogen replacements that I was running. The only gripe so far is while the horizontal spread is quite nice, the vertical cutoff seems to be less sharp than the OEM bulb. With a lot of inexpensive aftermarket LED replacements, beam scatter is an issue and these are no different. High beam reach was pretty comparable to stock, as expected since the LED position is close to OEM. Only installed tonight and ran them on a short trip. Time will tell if I give longevity more or less stars.

title: Better than $300 Maxtrax? Possibly
text: Unless you are hard core overlanding (ie not a weekend car camper) - these fit the bill. After watching countless reviews on overlanding youtube and reading reviews, I opted to get the Bunker Indust recovery boards. Compared to other budget traction boards these have a lower stack height; closer to Maxtrax - important since I need to roof mount them. Also, these came with a set of bright orange leashes so when the boards get buried in mud/snow you can easily retrieve them without much digging. Also these have a handy flat spot for a bottle jack or hi-lift. Time will tell if these do the trick. I read reviews how the teeth nubs are quickly worn away - that's from tire spinning, go slow and they won't melt off. Even if they do, my plan is to replace the nubs with stainless hex bolts; the hex heads make perfect nubs.

text: Set screws WILL vibrate loose sooner or later. Use BLUE Loctite to secure these. Manufacturer does not take much pride in Q/A, watch out for burrs and sharp edges left over from the factory. But for the money these work fine. You can spend 3x or more for CRG name brand, but no one but you will know the difference.

title: You like puzzles? Cause this is a puzzle.
text:
Unboxing:
Box came like it's been thrown around on a truck. The pieces are bagged but there is no padding or packing peanuts whatsoever. There are two bags of hardware; nuts and bolts. Unpacking the pieces... as expected they are made from the finest chineseium. A couple pieces are bent already. Also, when I went to sort out the bits, it appears it's already missing a knob.

Assembly:
Do you like puzzles? You'd better, because there are no instructions Luckily I am a little bit mechanical and was able to kind of sort it out. The captive nuts obviously fit into the C-channels. However, the corner pieces were the most challenging. As seen in the photos you need tiny hands to assemble the metal reinforcements inside the plastic piece, and semi-assemble them before sliding them onto the channels.

Once pieced together... loosen but don't remove the screws. Then, jiggle the assembled rack to square it up, since there is a lot of play. Snug the screws down again, then just to make sure, loosen them and measure from corner to corner diagonally in an X pattern, If both dimensions are equal, tighten down the screws.

Mounting:
The rack has simple plates that fit into the side channels. And the U bolts are meant to fit on a roof rack. However the side channels are pretty much at the ends of my roof rails, so the supplied U bolts did not fit around my crossrails. I had to hit up the hardware store for larger U bolts. Once centered I tightened down the rack to my roof bars.. the thin metal mounting plates immediately started to bend, as can be seen. The mounting plates adjust fore and aft, but you better have 34" of side to side spread on your cross bars. Oh and another thing.. this DOES NOT come with cross bars like the photo. If you have aero bars the maximum width must be less than 2.25in wide and 1.5in high or the stock ubolts won't fit.

TL/DR version: Pretty lightweight (150lbs capacity) - thin aluminum and poor quality. You get the idea.. for what this costs don't expect high quality fit and finish. The pros? I didn't have to drill out new holes, and only mild swearing at the shoddy quality.

*UPDATE*
Usage review:
I took the car out on the road this weekend to see how this rack was at speed. The wind noise was acceptable, given this does not come with a wind deflector like Yakima or Thule. Not sure if you could rig one up.. I suppose you could. The aerodynamic profile of the front cross member kept the noise down. But forget about tiliting up the little "handle" - it made quite a whistling noise with my sunroof open.

The front/back orientaton of the load bars reduce wind noise, but now you have to think about how to strap things down without sliding.

A few suggested improvements: replace the thin mounting plates with thicker steel, because you are pretty sure to keep bending them each time you use the rack. Also, use lock washers on the u-bolts especially if you drive rough roads.

title: Ok so far - Triumph Bonneville installation. Soft lens though
text: I bought this headlight for a custom build on my 09 Bonneville Thruxton. Unboxing: The headlight came well protected in a foam encased box. In addition to the lamp unit, there was a bag with various wiring harness adapters. The instructions were generic, as it made mention of wiring up to DRL lights, even though the unit I ordered only had wring for the main H4 harness. I might order another with the DRL, because the stock Thruxton has a small running lamp two wire light, but no big deal this time. Installation: After removing the stock headlight from the motorcycle, I proceeded to take apart the trim bezel. The Sunpie unit has three U shaped centering lugs on the edge - these are supposed to align with the retaining ring. However for the Triumph, the Sunpie lugs are too tall, so the ring did not fit flush against the light. I had to grind / bevel these lugs with a Dremel. Aside from that, the Sunpie is plug and play. One caution however, the polycarbonate lens is pretty soft. During installation I peeled off the plastic shipping tape too soon, and bumping the lens against my workbench while I was fiddling with the fit, I already got some micro scratches that I’m going to have to polish out. Can’t vouch for night performance yet - I haven’t had a chance to ride with it.

The yellow is distinct and cuts through bad weather. They look nice and different, so it's noticeable and unique. However after using those gas station squeegees to clean the lights, there are microscratches and halos starting to form. I will probably peel these off after the winter season.
** three months in ** Review update. Still on the car. I used this all winter and it has not clouded over, lifted, or faded one bit. As for the microscratches ,I got rid of them using Plexus plastic polish and they’re fine.

The adhesive didn't seem that tacky, but once I squeegeed it and USED HEAT to set the edges and the surface, it holds up just fine. It cut sharply with knifeless tape. One negative, I noticed it scuffed readily, some of the black areas smudged. That leads me to think this is cheaper calendared vinyl instead of more expensive cast vinyl.

I was impressed when the package eventually arrived, it comes in a carrying case with a pair of white gloves, car charger, separate battery, charge cable, and nozzle attachment. This combination keeps my engine and intake valves completely silent and stopped the valve cover gasket leaks. Should have returned these before I opened them. You can see the 2 small rubber bushings in the picture. It came with the larger bellow boots and abutment clips.

title: Missing rubber sleeves that are usually part of the kit
text: Came with the abutment clips. They fit. Came with the slide pin grease boots. They fit but were super tight. What it did not come with is the rubber grooved sleeves that go on one on of the 2 caliper slide pins on each caliper. The rubber sleeve that goes down into the caliper bracket hole. These are wear items. The rubber hardens or swells and causes seizing. A disc brake caliper hardware kit should include these rubber wear items as they are part of the hardware. I had to buy a Carlson brand hardware kit to get them. Disappointing to get my parts in and have my car in pieces to not be able to do them.

title: Alternate use for small convertible
text:
Purchased to use as very short term sun shade for my small 2 seater convertible (when parked at restaurant for lunch, etc). I recommend adding a short tether.
To use as a top sunblock, you must open the slit meant for the rear mirror and velcro it in place with umbrella above. Position the sun visors at 90° and rest the long edge with slit on the visors & above rear mirror. Velcro the slit with no slack around the mirror, then place the opposite edge on top of your headrests. My car has a flip-up console & I measured & tied a short piece of 225 paracord to the handle's strap (or use base of pole), added a stopper knot to the other end. Place the knot in the console & close the cover. This will help if a slight breeze attempts to flip the umbrella - it won't blow off, but the edge resting on your seatbacks may drop down into your cockpit (seat area will stay covered).
If you opt to put windows up - I recommend the ends of the short sides are kept inside the vehicle. Can be removed & stored behind seat while seated in vehicle.

title: Stops electricity in its tracks!

Although, if your car is parked somewhere that you can reach a plug, like in your garage, then the battery tender approach is better. Using the switch, the car forgets all of your settings, but that doesn't happen with a battery tender. However, if your car is parked out on the street, for example, then this switch is the perfect solution.

title: Great for a pandemic

My wife and I have 4 cars (for various historical reasons), and even before the pandemic I had troubles keeping all the batteries charged. When the pandemic hit, I started working from home, and we almost never go anywhere. We really just need 1 car these days, and my battery charging problem got a lot worse. Sometimes I would spend about 90 minutes on a Sunday just driving the different cars to charge them up. Huge pain!

These battery chargers are awesome. I just keep two of the cars in the garage all the time, each with one of these chargers. They work great. I can let the cars sit for months without a problem.

I couldn't really use this for the car I park out on the street, though, because I didn't want to run an extension cord out there across the sidewalk. For that one, I got a battery disconnect switch that mounts easily on the negative terminal. It works great for keeping the battery from running down over time (due to the always-on electronics in the car). However, I strongly prefer these chargers because using the battery disconnect switch wipes out all the settings.

title: Interesting concept - Complex installation
text:
The Tire Pressure Monitoring System is a great idea. While some newer cars have something like this built in, it's great for older cars and would be ideal for an RV or trailer to prevent any issues on a long trip. The car on which I've used the system has steel valve stems, so I haven't had any issues with losing air pressure or damage to the valves.

The thing I liked the least was the installation. There is no way I could have figured out how to install the system from the documentation supplied. I had to get help from someone who is very familiar with the set up of electronics, such as navigation systems, and even he had to muddle through to figure out how to complete the set up due to the poor documentation. One issue we had is that one of the tires we wanted to monitor was already low in pressure and the system wouldn't pick that tire up during the set up.

I like the design of the system itself. The monitor can be closed while driving, and then the driver only needs to worry about it if the green light changes to yellow or red. When the car is stopped, the screen can be reviewed to view the details on whatever problem is being detected. In addition, the monitor will sound an alarm for any of the "red" warnings.

I have found it to be a useful system and would definitely find it useful for an RV or if hauling a trailer. (Note: The manual says in some cases a "repeater" accessory is needed if a vehicle is over a certain length or something is being towed.)

title: Be kind to your diesel in winter
text: Bought at Autozone for $20 cheaper. Have a 97 dodge 3500 diesel dually up here in Wisconsin. Terrible cold starts, terrible. Got this a week ago and crawl under the front of the truck each day to apply or remove this from the oil pan, (no where else will it fit) and my truck starts MUCH MUCH easier. I don't like crawling under the truck, I'm a 50y/o woman, but I'll do it everyday for the fine results I get. It's light and easy to remove, the magnets aren't too strong to make it difficult to remove, nor would I expect that it'd stay put while driving, hence the daily application. I do recommend this product if you have limited choices of heater applications. Just check your local auto parts store to save money. One more thing, I apply it when I get home and leave it on until I use the truck again, so I don't know a how long it would take to heat up cold oil to make starting improved. Remember, Cummins diesel take 12 quarts of oil, double that of regular engines, so maybe a smaller engine could be warmed up in a few hours. Blessings!

title: Perfect for our Toyota Tacoma, perfect for saving money and the planet!
text:
Our trash and recycling pickup service has been going up and up and up, and their service has been getting less and less reliable. After going more than two weeks now without a trash pickup and a month with recyclables spilling out everywhere, we’ve decided we’re going to start hauling off our own trash. We only have about three bags of household trash per month, which we will have to take to the landfill, but we have a lot of recyclables and there is a 24-hour recycling drop-off less than a mile away from us. I work most of our cardboard into the garden as mulch with woodchips on top, but there is still a lot of loose stuff that we put in four small open-top plastic garbage cans we keep in our kitchen.

We needed something to keep these loose recyclables from blowing out of the truck, and after looking at all the different cargo net offerings, I decided to get this one. It costs more than some of the others, but it’s well worth the cost. It’s very high quality and should last a long, long time—and it will have paid for itself in a little more than a month of hauling our own trash instead of using Republic.

Even though this cargo net is probably overkill for our purposes, I thought it was important that the coverage be complete and the grid holes small enough to keep smaller loose items from blowing out. I am really impressed with how well-made and easy to use this cargo net is. The high-quality carabiner clips can hook to the rings in the bottom of our truck bed liner, and the plastic hooks can secure the net in places where there are no hooks but there are edges (like the part of the bed closest to the cab). The net stows tidily in its plastic carrying case when not in use and fits behind the bench seat of our truck, so we can also use it secure groceries we pick up curbside. I am also much more likely now to pick up my neighbors’ bagged leaves to use in my garden; in the past, I’ve been reluctant to get the ones filled up to the top of the paper leaf bags because leaves blow out of the bags on my way home.

So, all around, this cargo net is a great value!

title: A good gauge, but I wish it held the reading slightly longer
text:
I'm glad I was given this digital tire pressure gauge in exchange for my honest review, because I've got to drive about 850 miles in a week and this helped me discover that my tires are badly inflated and unbalanced. Not safe for long distance highway driving!

I like the feel of this tire gauge in the hand and I like that you can hang it up. It comes with the battery already installed, and it's very quick to use. If it ever gets uncalibrated, calibration is also quick; just stick it to the tire a second and release it and it calibrates automatically. I had no trouble using it on my truck's tires that have the air valve recessed inside the hub cabs.

Two things prevent me from giving this five stars. First, if you aren't angled totally straight to the little air valve, it catches on the valve just long enough to release some of the air you just put in as you try to remove it. I guess that's something you get the hang of after a while. The main thing, though, is that it resets to zero too quickly for somebody with old eyes and/or an aging memory. If it held just a second or two longer, I'd like it better. As it stands, I will make DP do the checking because I don't have long enough to commit the reading to short-term memory before it's gone. It's handy that it does reset itself, however, and the display is quite readable once you remove it from the tire.

title: I use it on Costco stock-up days in my truck bed

DP always packs items up close to the cab, but I because I'm so short and the sides of the truck are so high, I can't do that without having to climb up into the truck bed. Using this, I can open up the back of the truck and load things in toward the back, positioning this organizer in first as far as I can push it and still be able to grab it to pull it out, then stacking the heavier boxes of cans on either side. This makes a nice sturdy wall that keeps anything else I load in closer to the back from sliding toward the cab when I'm driving. Works great!

I got this trunk organizer at a discounted price in return for my honest review. I also received a free trashbag holder at the same time. I had to come back to see the product description to see what that extra thing was for, because I couldn't for the life of me figure out how it was supposed to snap onto the trunk organizer! It's a good thing to keep to stuff plastic grocery bags into, then return to the truck to have on hand when I shop at stores that use plastic bags; this way, I can ask them to reuse the bags—that and use them for trash in the truck.

UPDATE: Even though I have not lifted this trunk organizer by the handles, I have used the handles to slide it over when not packed very heavily. Already one of the handles has come loose. I'm knocking off a star for that.

title: For me, better than the SpotBot
text:
About five years ago, I had a Bissell SpotBot, and I really hated that thing. (Maybe they've been redesigned now, so take what I'm about to say with a grain of salt.) The SpotBot's selling point was that it was hands-free, but when it finished cleaning, it would beep. And beep. And beep. And beep. Nag, nag, nag until I stopped whatever I was doing and climbed up or down the stairs and picked it up and put it away. I liked that it did a good job of cleaning, but it was annoying as heck. And then, within a very short time, but not so short I could return it, it broke down.

Compared to the SpotBot, this Rug Doctor portable spot cleaner is wonderful. It's a good solid build, and it's not nearly as noisy as my old SpotBot was. One thing I really, really, really like about it is the size of the cleaning wand. I'm sure most dog owners can relate to this: My chiweenie, Bingo, knows I don't want him to have accidents in the house. So if he has to throw up or has diarrhea, he tends to find a place under an end table to do it so I won't know about it. (Yeah, right.) These are precisely the places a SpotBot won't work because it is too large to fit without having to move furniture. The Rug Doctor portable spot cleaner wand allows me to get in there and deal with it. I also like the fact that I can get the cleaning solution at any grocery store that rents the big Rug Doctors—and so many of them do. It does a good job. It's convenient. And so far, knock on wood, it's going to be dependable. And then it tucks into a closet without taking up very much space. Nice.

title: Good design for resale, functional and fun
text:
Outdoorsmen and -women needing to travel light, commuters, and parents who want to always be prepared are probably the target end-users for this product, but the packaging of the InstaCloth as sold here on Amazon is really designed for resale. That will be my focus for this review.

Although somewhat flimsy and prone to coming apart (but easily fortified with a small piece of clear packing tape to the bottom), the cardboard box containing 12 individually boxed foil and plastic blister-paks is designed for enticing, efficient display of the product. The box is designed with tear-off side flaps and a top flap that folds back into the box, creating an eye-catching standalone mini display.

Each individual cardboard box (holding an 8-pak of the cloth tablets) includes a clear plastic hanging tab like those you see on products hung about in grocery stores. With bold color and type, iconographic usage suggestions, and succinct and clear instructions (even the perfectly placed caveat "CAUTION! Do NOT place in mouth or consume!"), the packaging is perfect to entice impulse buyers to try the product. The InstaCloth IS novel and interesting. If priced right, people might pick up one package just for the fun of it.

I can see these InstaCloths being a hit beside cash registers in convenience stores, camping and sports retailers, sit-and-wait car washes, office supply stores, and anywhere commuters or travelers might shop for other items and wind up waiting in a checkout line. They could be used as inexpensive stocking stuffers, party favors, or even (with the right crowd) gag gifts. In a restaurant, a parent (or the proprietor or server) might do a "magic act" to quiet a rowdy child who is disturbing other customers. Dipped into a water glass, an InstaCloth tablet would be perfect for cleaning up a child's sticky face and fingers after a meal where most paper napkins would fall apart. And as far as the "splash of water" goes, I'd think spilled coffee or soda would work just fine to unfurl these little "pills."

The product could be further improved by perforating the blister-paks so the individual cloths can be broken off and carried separately—tucked into a lunchbox, perhaps, or divided up among children at a birthday party.

text: My daughter asked me if I could get her car into our shop at the used car dealership where I work. It seems her 2013 Kia Optima SX-Limited had a low beam that went out. So she went to the KIA dealership that has serviced it for many years to get it replaced. (they should be publicly named and shamed, but I won't) They told her it would be over $750 to replace the low beams on both sides (they should be done it pairs). After she stopped herself from falling over...she asked why so much?  Well the special HID bulbs are very expensive, like over  $150 ea. and you have to remove the whole front end and grille of the car to remove the headlight housings to get them out, and install the new ones. She correctly deferred and told them she would get back to them after some research. Then she called me. I thought that it was a rip-off in process and in less than 10 mins. found these EXACT fit bulbs on Amazon, using the "Amazon Garage"  tool to be sure I had the correct part. Then I did a quick search on the internet via Google and Youtube, finding a video that showed these bulbs, on that car being changed out easily, they did remove the headlights and front portion, but I didn't think it was even necessary. I told her to bring her car to me, I ordered and got these bulbs the next day, for under $30 a pair. I lifted her hood, reached behind the headlight housing (driver's side) and removed the rear cover as I just twisted it off, unclipped the wire holder, unplugged the bulb, took it out, plugged in the new, (turned on the car and lights to test it was on before clipping and putting the rear cover back on)  and dropped the hood.  DONE, in less than 10 minutes. The color temperature and brightness were identical and just as good as the factory bulb on the passenger side.  I didn't do both because these lights last for 5 yrs or more, if one fails again, I can always do the other and she has a spare now.  So, watch out for the predatory dealer or shops and save yourself some huge money. JFGI  "Just friggin Google It" and order up from Amazon.

title: Glad I didn't listen to "30 year Master Tech" and throw away mh car...
text: Great low price, fast shipping! (arrived a day early)  I work at a Used Car dealership with an in-house service dept. (3 techs one Service mgr) About 2 weeks ago my car (2000 VW Jetta TDI sedan witj only 289,000 miles) shifted erratically driving in to work. Finally it went only into 'limp' mode locking in 3rd gear, unless I shifted the selector manually. Our 'master tech' service manager scanned OBD codes and said a incorrect gear ratio code  meant my car was toast, throw it away and buy a new one.. it was a $1 car. I scanned it and found one code for "Transmission output shaft speed sensor no signal". Googled it and found symptoms identical to mine. The sensor wire it seems runs from the sensor to the ECM routing under the battery.  Hmmm... I thought, just had my shop replace my battery 3 weeks ago because the case split and puked acid out under the car and on our parking lot. J figured maybe acid ate the sensor cable under the battery box. Bought this part for literally 1/10th what local stores could order it in for, and had them install it. No acid damage to the old part, but it WAS nearly severed where it was chafing under the battery box having been improperly routed.  Problem solved. Glad it was relatively minor. Shifts like new.

title: Works Well But Follow Directions and Video
text: You can read a whole bunch of reviews about how this product does or doesn't work.  Key to success is going to the Permatex website and clicking on their Video Demo Online link.  Choose the "Permatex® Complete Rear Window Defogger Repair Kit" video.  They've partnered with GM, but the key here is that they show many more steps than the back of the package.  The first part of the video is about the grid repair, you can skip to about the middle of the video to where they show the tab repair portion (unless you need to fix your grid as well, but then, you'd be on a different Amazon web page).  So what was my key to success: preparation, preparation, ... you get the idea.  First, remove the tab from the pigtail of the wiring harness.  On my 2004 Ford Taurus, even that chore wasn't easy, it was pretty well locked in.  Once out, you really have to get all the old adhesive off the mating surface of the tab.  This took about 15-20 minutes of going slow with (in my case) a metal file to knock off the big chunks and then switching to the fine sandpaper called out in the video.  Didn't see that on the back of the package?  That step isn't there, but is essential.  I also lighted sanded the window glass mounting area (very lightly), just to get rid of any roughness where the tab was previously fastened before it tore loose.  Then you need to clean the surface of both the tab and the window glass mating surface with rubbing alcohol.  Didn't see that step either, right?  Watch the video!!  So I broke out our trusty bottle of 70% IPA and a clean paper towel, soaked the towel, and meticulously wiped down the surface of the tab and the glass where it would mate, a number of times, allowing the IPA to dry / evaporate quickly in between.  Don't touch the tab side after you've cleaned it with the rubbing alcohol, or you'll transfer oil from your fingers.  At this point, you're ready to apply the tab to the window glass area it separated from.  On our Taurus, there's a sizable block of the reddish brown conductive material on the rear glass to apply it to, including the small area where it broke away from.  DON'T PUT IT BACK DIRECTLY ON THE SMALL SECTION IT SEPARATED FROM!  It might work, but it's cheap insurance to place it above, below, or to the side of that "gap" in the remaining conductive material.  To apply the tab to the glass, there's a two part solution, one is the adhesive contained in the foil pouch, and the second part is the conductive material in the little bag.  Knead the conductive material first, a lot.  Do this on a warm day, not a 28F day (I did ours in our garage in late spring, about 60F).  If it is too cold, the two part adhesive won't cure readily -- then you'll read about the folks whose tab "fell off".  If you are in the middle of winter and try this repair, I suggest you consider bringing your hair dryer out to the car and heating up the glass mounting area to room temp (70-75F).  That will aide in the curing process.  After kneading the conductive material bag, open the foil pouch with the adhesive (and as they warn you, don't touch the adhesive).  Apply that to both the tab mounting surface AND the window glass area you'll be applying the tab to.  WAIT AT LEAST TWO MINUTES, BUT NOT MORE THAN FIFTEEN.  Didn't see that step?  Watch the video!!  It won't look wet, but it has applied the adhesive to those two areas.  I waited 3 minutes before applying a blob of the conductive material to the tab surface (on top of the adhesive you can't see).  Then I pressed it into place on a CLEAN part of the conductive material block on the rear window.  Press and hold for 1 minute.  Then wait 24 hours for the two part system to cure before plugging the wire pigtail connector back onto the tab.  This worked first time for me, but I probably spent an hour total reading the directions on the package, watching the video 2x, writing down all the steps from the video, and actually performing the repair.  The tab is holding, the defroster grid works, and the repair is effective. By the way, the reason for the 4 star rating and not 5 is the fact that Permatex doesn't refer to the video on their package, and without watching the video, your odds of success are diminished significantly, because the limited instructions on the back of the package are probably not enough to ensure success.  But now you know the tricks!  Good luck!

title: Amazing product, easy install and back on the road!
text: I can’t say enough good about this product! This is an item you won’t know you need until you can’t put the car in gear or get it started. Mine was on Lexus RX300. You only need to remove the wood trim piece around the shifter - use a putty knife to pop it off. Then remove the wire connectors from the power plug, heated seat switch and traction off switch.  You can reach it all easy, car in neutral is the most slack. Remove the old pieces from the hole in the cable connection, grease the pin and the new bushing and push it on- slotted side goes first. Then push it onto the shifter pin and your done. Reassemble the trim piece, putting the wires back on the switches. Your done 15-30 minutes.  Also I shoved rags in the abyss because you do not want to drop this little thing and go looking for it!  Might be a little pricey for what you get, but well engineered and worth every dollar.

The 3M PPS system is the greatest advancement in spray painting in many years.

It solves so many nagging problems:
1. Gets rid of the paint cup, which is a true pain to clean
2. The sealed liner collapses like a bag in a baby formula bottle. This means you can turn the gun at any angle without drips or venting. This may be its best feature.
3. The sealed, collapsing liner means you can put a cap on the cup to store paint temporarily (say, overnight).
4. You can either clean and reuse the liner and filter/top quick disconnect adapter, or throw it away. I clean it if I'm spraying water based clear coatings or clear solvent-based coatings that clean easily. Got maybe 6-7 uses out of a 6-oz unit. If the paint is just too messy, throw it away. Shot some black Rustoleum today and just didn't want a ton of black paint thinner to deal with. By throwing the cup away, I only had to clean the gun's throat and air cap. Took about 2-3 ounces to clean the gun. And talk about quick. Cleaning that darned cup takes the most time. Eliminate cleaning the cup and it's a quick job. I put the thinner in a 4-oz squeeze bottle to dispense the thinner into the gun's throat. No muss, no fuss.

This 10-cup kit works out to about $4.30 per cup. A little steep but convenience has a price.

If you're using your own gun, you'll have to buy a stainless steel adapter to put on the gun that the PPS attaches to with a quarter turn. Get the adapter here for your particular gun -- [[ASIN:B000N9RWTK 3M 16003 PPS Adapter 2]]

You also must purchase the 22 oz. PPS Mixing Cup and Collar. These flexible liners need to go inside a reusable, sturdier structure. [[ASIN:B000AO0MTA 3M PPS Mixing Cup and Collar, Standard, 22 ounce (650 mL), 16001]]. Another $28.

I don't know what I was thinking buying these lids/liners and the cup/collar separately. Should have simply purchased the 3M kit. 6 liners and lids like these and the outer cup/collar for way less. [[ASIN:B01LRIQ0YS 3M 16172 PPS Starter Kit, (Pack of 6) (Standard Size 22 fl. oz. 6-Pack Lid and Liner, 1 Cup and Collar with 200 Micron Filters) by PPS]]

I really like the 6-oz mini cup for small jobs, but just got these Standard ones too, for larger jobs. The Standard is 22 ounces -- 2/3 of a quart. It's bigger than I thought. And there's one larger size available too.

My first, 6-oz, kit came with small red plastic caps that I can put on the liner cups. This Standard, 10 cup/lid set did not have any caps. The caps are helpful if you want to take the cup off the gun, clean the gun and store the paint in the cup overnight.

Great system.

title: Adapter Number 2 for Generic HVLP; Adapter 18 Fits But Doesn't Work With Apollo 5105
text:
Got two adapters: the No 2 adapter fits my generic HVLP (Harbor Freight, Lowes, Home Depot, etc) with a gravity feed cup.

Not exactly sure what the threads are officially, but they are very close to 5/8" across, measuring with a caliper.

I attached it to the gun after wrapping some teflon tape around the threads so there would be zero leaks. The gravity fed PPS system is fantastic. Love it.

Update Notes on Number 18:

The Number 18 adapter fits my bottom cup fed Apollo 5105 HVLP. It has 3/8" straight threads with a convex dome flare-type metal to metal seal inside. Designed to receive a fluid hose connector from a pressure pot. Seals nicely without teflon tape. Adapter is about 3" long and holds the cup low, out of the way of the trigger. Someone here said the Number 34 is the same, but shorter.

UNFORTUNATELY the 5105 gun requires a pressure cup to push paint up to the tip. This Number 18, though it fits, simply does not deliver any paint from the PPS cup because the gun requires pressure in the cup. Had to send the Number 18 back. The Number 2 on a gravity fed gun works great.

I paired these adapters with the 3M 6-oz Mini Cup PPS collapsible inner insert, lids and plugs [[ASIN:B000ANUHAA 3M 16114 PPS Mini Size Kit with 200 Micron Filters]] with the 200 micron filters in each insert, and the outer cup and retaining collar [[ASIN:B000RHWLUI 3M 16115 PPS Mini Cup and Collar]].

I can now invert the gun with no dripping and clean up faster with the 3M system.

Both adapters are beautifully machined stainless.

title: Designed For Rollaway Drawers, Not For Carrying A Set Around
text:
These wrench organizers are for use in an 18" front-to-back rollaround toolbox drawer. They really aren't designed to be carried to a job or thrown in the back of a truck loose. They hold up to fifteen wrenches that are in a steel drawer.

The unit is 16-7/8" long including the plastic loop on one end. If you cut the loop off, it's 16-1/2" long. While one of my rollarounds has 18" front-to-back drawers, the other rollaround has drawers that are 16" front-to-back. These will not fit as delivered.

Fortunately, the plastic end caps can be easily pried off the extruded aluminum channel of the main body. This allowed me to cut an inch off the aluminum with a metal-cutting cutoff saw and reassemble to my desired length. See the pictures.

The red or blue anodized aluminum channel (one for SAE, one for Metric -- you'll have to paint the metal some other color for your Whitworth spanners, sadly) is obviously non-magnetic. Strong magnets in the plastic end caps hold the aluminum to the floor of your steel drawer. Somewhat weaker magnets in the sliding and angled wrench holders hold the wrenches in place so you can easily see the sizes and give ready access. The wrench holders are 2" wide.

For really large (long) end wrenches they recommend you place two of these units side by side as the magnetic holders are only 2-1/16" wide. A really long wrench will no doubt tilt off..

Came recommended by my professional mechanic brother-in-law who uses them all day, every day.

Just don't expect to lift a full set out and carry it off. One or two at a time only.

title: Great Addition and I Really Like It, But Needs More Engineering
text:
I have a tilt-gate trailer like the one they picture except it has 2-7/16" OD round tubular top rails, not flat rails.

The yellow spring housings come in two pieces to allow a shorter shipping box. You butt them up and then bolt them down, two bolts for each piece of tubing.

However, there's nothing to align the two yellow tubes together. Thus flat-bottomed square tubes are precariously sitting on top of round tubular rails. You are instructed to drill oversized holes through the mounting rails. This allows you to reposition the square tubes before tightening them down, but also allows the two tubes to move slightly as they absorb eventual road vibrations. The yellow spring housing tubes can become misaligned after a while. If that happens, the long garage-style springs inside the housing hang up on the misaligned tube edges in the middle and "boing" as they slip off.

They should have welded ears onto the tubes that force the tubes to stay aligned or be hinged so that they are mechanically aligned after installation.

Also, be aware that the threaded bolts are all metric. The carriage bolts look like they're 5/16-18 thread, and say so in the instructions, but they are not. The gate-mounting bolts look like they are 1/2-13, but they are not.

The carriage bolts supplied are not long enough to go through my 2-7/16" tubular top rails. I had to purchase eight new galvanized carriage bolts (didn't want them to rust). That's when I discovered the threads were not SAE. The supplied nuts did not fit properly.

One of the great features of this type of trailer is that you can fold the gate forward onto the bed to get it out of the wind for significantly less drag and better mileage. If you employ their permanently-attached cable system and its 6" long metric 1/2" bolts, you can never fold the gate inward -- the bolts make the gate too wide to fit inward.

If you look at the pictures, you'll see that I rigged up a different system using shorter, custom-cut 1/2-13 threaded rod with locknuts, washers and a hitch pin. This allows me easily to remove the cables and still fold the gate inward on return highway trips when empty or lightly loaded. I now have the best of both worlds: an easy-lifting gate and an inwardly foldable gate.

Finally, a word on the springs. Since they have no idea how heavy or large your ramp-gate is, they supply two coaxial springs that are really strong. Two springs, one inside the other for each side, comprise the default setup. This means you have five spring combinations to choose from.
1. Both inner and outer springs on both sides, if your gate is really heavy.
2. Both outer springs (no inner springs) on both sides, if the gate is heavy.
3. One outer spring on one side, both inner/outer springs on the other side if the gate is a bit less heavy.
4. One inner spring on one side, one outer spring on the other side.
5. One inner spring on both sides.

You test the gate using various combinations and S hooks until you're happy with the balance.

The problem is that to get the springs apart so you can use only the inner spring, you have to cut the outer spring's loop and pull the larger outer spring off the pair. This renders the spring almost unusable if you change your mind. It's a bit confusing in print. Weigh your combinations carefully before cutting.

Out of the box and per side, you can attach the cable to 1) both springs or 2) the outer, larger spring. You can't attach to the just the smaller, inner spring by itself.

Because my gate is fairly light, the combination I needed was a single inner spring on one side and one outer spring on the other side. I cut the large outer spring off with an angle grinder. You'd need a very large bolt cutter, or maybe a hacksaw, to cut the spring. But spring steel is very tough. Don't know if a hacksaw would make it.

Anyway, now that the gate is balanced fairly well, it's simply a matter of picking it up with my toe and it rises easily into position to be locked off. Very handy indeed.

title: Sturdy, Compact Lug Wrench
text:
Got this for my utility trailer tool box should I need to change the tire on the road. Folds compactly so I can put it in a standard tool box with the scissor jack, its crank handle and some gloves.

Like the rest of the wrench, the sliding sleeves are strong steel and snap together to form an X. The sleeves are like socket wrenches -- very strong. I like an X-shaped lug wrench because it gives excellent leverage and spins the nuts on or off quickly.

The multiple-sized sockets are good because the spare uses one size nut and the trailer's lugs are larger. This fits both. Comes in a fairly durable clear plastic bag with a snap closure for storage. Nicely chrome plated.

title: Wish the Vertical Offset were higher
text:
This device bolts sturdily to almost any trailer frame as long as it's got a rectangular cross section.
I mounted it on the tongue as far back as possible to keep weight off the hitch. I have a 15" spare. My trailer rides pretty low. With this mount bolted as high as possible I only have about 4" of ground clearance before the spare rubs the ground. This only happens coming off driveways onto a high-crowned street, but it happens. I know it's happening because the vinyl spare tire cover is ripped on the bottom from hitting the pavement.

Some improvements: the bolts supplied that hold the tire onto the mount are fine thread 1/2"-20, that fit the lugnuts supplied. I found that it's difficult to hold the tire up and put the bolt thorough both the mount and rim at the same time. What I wanted was for the bolts to stay on the mount by themselves as if the were a hub. I bought two 1/2" jam nuts at the hardware store and permanently mounted the lugs to the mount in the hole pattern suitable for my rim. Now when I remove or install the spare, it comes off and goes on much easier.

The lug nuts that come with the mount use a 3/4" socket to fit. This may be different than the nuts on your trailer so be sure to have a lug wrench that fits both.

title: Removes All Hitch Movement -- No More Rattles
text:

Pulls the stinger up against the hitch and really makes it solid. The stinger is pivoting up and down on the 1/2" hitch pin otherwise (or the 5/8" pin with a 2" hitch) and side to side too, and rattles on every bump.

With this little tightener the ball, stinger and hitch feel like they're welded together as a single unit. Hauling a trailer is much quieter now.

Only problem is that you need a wrench to remove the ball and stinger, so it stays on the car longer than usual. Small price to pay for a solid hitch,

Great, heavy-duty device.

title: Good for Long Term Storage
text:
I found out my ancient 30- or 40-year old totally analog 6-12V charger inherited from my dad decades ago does terrible things to a car battery.

If left on "trickle" for a week or two or four, it actually boils the water out of a maintenance-free battery. I killed one battery. Then I almost killed my truck's battery. It barely started my Ranger and it's only a year old. I popped the caps off and, sure enough, I could see the tops of the lead plates. Not enough water. I added distilled water to cover the plates and put this Battery Tender charger on it overnight and in the morning the truck started like the battery was brand new.

I'm not saying this charger saved the battery. I think adding water before the battery was destroyed did the trick. What I'm saying is that if you need to keep your battery on maintenance charge because you don't drive it much or it has to sit for long periods, this charger will not boil the water out and kill the battery.

title: For upper Power Steering fitting of 2005 Acura TL
text:
This larger O-ring fits the upper, pressure, side of the 2005 Acura TL power steering pump. It's under the fitting that has two 10mm bolts, not the lower, low-pressure fitting that's held on via a single 10mm bolt that attaches to the reservoir.

The lower one is the one that most likely goes bad and turns black from the original orange color. If you pump whines, it's possibly because the lower O-ring has gone bad. That part number is 91345-RDA-A01 - O-Ring (13.0X1.9)

title: Fits 2005 Acura TL low pressure side to the Reservoir, not the top pressure side
text:
For my 2005 Acura TL, this is the o-ring that fits on the side (not the top) of the pump that connects to the hose that goes to the reservoir. 13mm x 1.9mm red. If the pump is whining, it's getting air into the system when it's cold until it warms up. Removing the fitting with a single 10mm bolt that is reached with a right angle 10mm socket reaching between the serpentine belt reveals the O-ring. But it will on be on the hose end. It will be inside the pump. If the ring is black, it means it's cooked and old. Remove the ring with a pick or other pointed tool that you can reach inside with to pull it out carefully. Discard and replace with this orange ring.

NOTE: the upper pressure side O-ring that's under the top fitting that's held with two 10mm bolts is different from this ring. It's black and is 14.8mm x 1.9mm and and a different part number: W0133-1928135

title: Anything is better than my 2008 Edge's battery clamp
text:
The battery finally died and I needed to change it for the first time. Should have taken all of 45 minutes, including buying the new battery. Done it many times. The common lead cable clamp has been adequate for, oh, about one hundred years.

But in 2008 Ford decided to replace the tried and true lead clamps with the most over-engineered contraption ever. My clamp is a folded copper (or copper plated) thingie with dual sliding wedges (?) that pull a steel strap across and through the clamp to tighten it. I assume it worked fine when new (I don't exactly test my battery clamp bolts on a regular basis) but after five years the bolt that pulls the little wedges together and the tightening strap were corroded into a single lump. No matter what, the bolt would not come loose. Spent a couple of hours trying to get the clamp to loosen.

And the way the clamp is designed, I don't think there's enough cable to cut it off and attach a new one.

This clamp set looks like a good fix, but means an extra couple of hours or more, plus doubles the cost of replacing a battery.

Ford, this is almost as boneheaded as reengineering the air conditioning hose connections on the Taurus so they leaked all the freon out every year.

It had a hinged door that opened but the hinges were very delicate plastic that lasted less then a year, then broke so the hoses fell out while traveling. So I bought this new version, since I already had made a mounting bracket for the first version. THEY CHANGED THE MOUNTING HOLES!!. The new product had mounting hole roughly a quarter inch different. This means that you can’t even use the old mounting position since there is no way to move a self tapping screw hole just a little. text: Stay away from this product if you have a R410a system!  It is implied it works with any Freon, that may be true of the sealant material but not the tool. It was easy enough to attach but the crimp connection from the AC low side port to the hose simply isn’t up to the task at R410a pressures, though the instructions indicate it can be used in systems with suction pressures above 100 psi - which R410a does. The instructions do recommend using a caulking gun to help inject the contents in higher pressure systems. However, even without attempting to inject the contents, the low side pressure blew the connector out of the hose. I had been doing my own AC work for years and when I first inspected this hose connection, I suspected it wouldn’t hold. So I was ready to quickly take it off the port and so lost a negligible amount of coolant.

title: I think it will be OK
text: This was interesting. I originally purchased the wrong size and needed to order this larger one. It has the same mounting process as the Camco 42145 screen - a weak loosely coiled spring that you hook onto the screen and then a rather useless tool that you are supposed to use to fish through the screen and hook to the vent louvers on the unit. I never got that far however. The screen is smaller then actually required and the actual unit it covers is a raised square chromed plate with a circular exhaust in the center. As a result of the screen size, it actually got hung up on the corners of the square plate and won't come off easily. I expect this will actually provide a better mount then the little weak springs so just left it there. I'll see if there are any issues over time but may just caulk it in place to be sure.

title: Not thrilled with the mounting hardware
text: This screen fit fine but the mounting equipment leaves a great deal to be desired. It relies on very weak, loosely wound metal springs that are supposed to connect to the screen on one side and then hook around the vents of the unit to hold them in place. They provide a tool to help you complete this hooking maneuver - which doesn't really work well. Since you have to open the panel on the RV and access the back side of the vents to actually hook these springs, it would have been far better to provide a long thin screw and flat washer that you could just push through the screen and attach to the vent. The current mounting is rather loose so I'm a bit nervous about how well it will remain in place. I suspect I will find a long screw or use some caulk and mount it more securely. Overall, assuming the screen actually prevents bugs from entering, it will be a good investment.

title: Installation was interesting
text: These are installed on the outside of the vents using zip ties. The zip ties seem to leave spaced between the screen and the plastic cover that are bigger then the screen openings. title: Good tool for occasional use.
text: This tool is just what I needed to use inside my metal building to hang shelves and provide anchor points to the hollow metal beams.  Unlike a stud-build structure, I cannot nail directly to the wall and needed something to provide anchor points.  The tool comes with a wide selection of mandrels and a starter box of rivets.  I purchased extra rivets in S.A.E. sizes as I'm not much on metric (personal preference).  Only downside, the instructions are less than ideal, they need to be written as if I never used a tool like this before (I hadn't). Also, bit sizes, for rivet holes, are given in metric sizes (1/4-20 is 9.1mm).  Since it's sold in America, an S.A.E. chart would be helpful. Being somewhat mechanically inclined, I figured out the nuances and, with practice was able to persevere.  Overall, well built and works as advertised once you learn how to set it up and make yourself a bit "cheat card".

title: Covers Ranger 500 but with modification.
text: I purchased this cover on 7/18/20 and have used it almost continually since then.  As some have said, this is a little large for the Polaris Ranger 500, even with my metal roof and homemade roof rack, I find that true.  Initially, water would pool in the bed, but the fix was to put 2-1gal. buckets upside down on the roof, one front and one back.  This tightened up things and caused water to drain correctly.  I must admit, I've gotten my money's worth out of this cover.  It has held up to the elements, being parked outside, for just over 2 years.  It is now showing some tearing at touch points (even though I've padded the machine there) and at the strap attachment and tie down holes.  I probably should have given it a couple of waterproofing treatments before long term service.  Truth be told, it's probably UV damage causing degradation.  The 4-star rating was for the "one size fits all" approach, but overall, this is a good product.

It's replacement time and I'll go with a different line due to the outer sleeve issues as that tends to catch on protrusions and kink making tears.  All-in-all, it served me well.

title: Buy with confidence
text:
I normally purchase the factory mats, so purchasing aftermarket was a new experience for me. Unboxing was uneventful and there was no discernible odor when I opened the box and removed the mats. I was pleased to discover that the fit was absolutely perfect for both front and rear, which is important for a guy with three very active grands. I like the high lipped edges, which appear to preclude the chances of anything less than a tsunami of liquid reaching the carpet at the rear of the mats. My only (very minor) gripe is that I discovered not all mats come with the latch cover discs for the front driver's mat. A handout in the box explains that not all mats are so equipped, but I can certainly get over that omission. I can recommend these for anyone with a 2019 Prius.
9 Month Update: After a spring and summer of use, I can endorse these mats as nothing short of a great purchase. They look as good as the day they came out of the box, and I can easily clean them with a scrub brush and a little soap. With the slickery finish, dirt and grime are removed without a trace. Do be aware the the carpet grippers on the back side of the mats are seriously sharp and a pair of gardening gloves are recommended when removing the mats from the car, lest you ventilate your fingers. One recommendation is to purchase and install red LED side marker bulbs and a set of 921 reverse light bulbs as long as you're going to be in there anyway. title: Easy installation
text: Good quality filter on par with the OEM filter, and you can't beat the price. I've purchased many cabin and engine air filters with the EPAuto brand and never encountered a problem. Replacement is literally a five minute (or less) job on a 2017 Toyota Corolla iM with the popular 1.8L engine. Pop the two clips that hold the housing closed on drivers side and passenger/firewall side of the filter housing, lift the upper housing and slip out the old filter (make sure to note which corner is squared off instead of rounded when you remove the old filter). Slip in the new filter, reinstall the upper air intake, snap those clips back into place and you're done. No need to remove hoses, wiring, or the air intake tube. Folks, this is one degree of difficulty higher than putting washer fluid in the reservoir. Put a reminder in your phone to replace it in a year or 15,000 miles and you're done. It you don't normally do work on your own car, this is a great way to start. Peace!

title: Really, Toyota?
text: These are inexpensive  replacement horns for our RAV4, but Toyota should be ashamed of the junky, weak, ineffective, and tinny Denso horns they install at the factory. I'm aware that the pennies add up when building a car, but these are a huge improvement for less than $20 retail. They compare favorably with the Hella Supertone horns I installed on my 2017 Corolla iM, but don't require a relay and are a direct replacement, including the power receptacle. Easy to install, requiring only a 10 and 12mm (wrench) socket, along with a small flat blade to pop the plastic retainers under the hood. I completed the job in about 30 minutes from start to finish, so this is an easy one. Highly recommended and a critical safety improvement for any car with factory Denso horns.

I suspect either the collet attaching to the  Caliper's petcock either wasn't able to form a proper seal or it was due to the junction where the tube entered the black plastic adapter lacking a hermetic seal. Regardless I was able to make it work, I just had to continuously draw fluid out until I closed the caliper's petcock to prevent air from getting back inside. Overall I'd recommend, people just have to be aware of plastic shavings in the reservoir and make sure if they have continuous bubbles, that they always have air pressure moving through the unit so as to make sure that air doesn't seep back into the caliper's petcock.
