exhaust and had no problems. But after i replaced the cat back portion of the Cobb exhaust with a Borla cat back there was a lot of miscellaneous noise coming from under the car. Initially i thought the exhaust flange bolts must have been loosening up but when i checked them they were tight. I was afraid i might have to re-install the Cobb cat-back to eliminate the noise until i decided to give these STI bushings a shot. They are significantly stiffer than the standard Subaru bushings which makes it quite a bit harder to install them. I used a little dishwashing detergent and a spray bottle to lubricate the holes in the bushings and the metal support posts they slide onto. These bushings have eliminated the annoying noises i had after i swapped cat-backs.

title: Great Value If You Need '04 STI Rotors

title: No Problems
text:
I used this along with the FJC 6909 vacuum pump to evacuate and charge an AC system i installed in my car that didn't have factory air. i wasn't sure if i needed the manual couplers that come with this or quick release couplers but this gauge set with manual couplers worked fine. the hoses were of good quality and were long enough. i paid a few bucks more over the cost of just the manifold set to get the nice carrying case.

the included instructions on how to evacuate and charge an AC system were adequate for a first-timer. just be very careful to make sure that the couplers are fully seated on your car's AC service ports and that they stay seated when you try to charge your system with refrigerant. my low side coupler was not initially fully seated on the service port. no R-134A escaped but it also would not flow into the system until i re-seated it and the schraeder valve got fully depressed.

title: Used It Once So Far And It Worked Well
text:
I used this to evacuate an AC system i installed in my car that didn't come with factory air. i ran the pump for about 45 minutes and my manifold gage indicated a vacuum of 21" Hg which was not as low as i was hoping for. i did some research online and found a chart which indicated that at my elevation (5,000') the best vacuum i could possibly get was ~25" Hg. the vacuum in my AC system held steady for a few days so i decided it was leak-free and it was safe to charge it with R134a. prior to charging the system with refrigerant i ran this pump for about another 30 minutes and was glad to see the system vacuum drop to 23" - 24" Hg (the day i did this was quite a bit warmer than the day when i originally evacuated the system).

i'm glad i bought this pump and a manifold and did it myself. i suspect an AC shop would have charged about half what i paid for this pump and an FJC 6766P manifold. so my net cost was pretty low and if i use it again i will break even and have the tools.

one thing to watch closely is the pump oil level sight glass. mine had used quite a bit of oil in less than 90 minutes of operation. you don't want to let the level get too low!

title: OK For Simple Flushing
text:
This works fine for simple flushing of car AC hoses and pipes that are out of the vehicle. It is not as good for flushing AC system components like an evaporator.

The problem is that you presurize the bottle through a schrader valve at the top of the bottle. Then you get a short duration burst of solvent to flush the hose or component. To remove the flush solvent you need an uninterrupted stream of air (or nitrogen). This is especially true for a component. This is difficult to do with this kit unless you have a helper hold the air compressor hose on the bottle's schrader valve while you hold the flush gun in place and pull the trigger.

If you will be flushing multiple components you'd be better off getting a kit that has a valve on the bottle inlet and a fitting that allows you to thread the air compressor output to the bottle inlet so you don't have to hold it. Then after you flush with solvent and the bottle is empty you can do an uniterrupted air purge for as long as you like.

I used about 20 ounces of flush solvent to clean a used evaporator and eight AC hoses and pipes before installing them in my car.

title: First One Broke Second One Worked Great
text:
This looked like it would be a great time saver by avoiding the need to remove the trailing arms from my cars ('97 Del Sol and '93 Civic) to replace the bushings.

I do not have a lift so i attempted this alone with the car on jackstands. I started on the drivers' side of my Del Sol by removing the toe adjusting bolt at the end of the compensating arm (I planned on getting an alignment anyway) as well as the two bolts that hold the trailing arm bushing in place. That was not adequate to drop the trailing arm far enough to remove the bushings so i also had to remove the upper arm outer bushing bolt and two parking cable bolts.

The first problem i had while trying to remove the driver side bushing (from the inside pushing it toward the outside of the car) was that the cylindrical spacer is not long enough to contact the circumference of the bushing's metal shell because the metal bar portion of the bushing is in the way. After trying several times i finally gave up and resorted to drilling and sawing away the rubber portion of the bushing so i could seat the spacer on the metal shell of the bushing.

It is difficult to place the tool properly while simultaneously holding the spacer and tightening the shaft that presses the spacer against the bushing shell. an extra set of hands would be very helpful for getting the tool ready to press the bushing out.

Now comes the bad part. the hooked arms of the tool are a little too wide to hold securely to the edges of the trailing arm. i tried rotating the tool so it would contact the widest dimension of the trailing arm but every time i tightened the shaft the tool would slip off the trailing arm. if the arms of the tool were about 4 mm closer together it would not have slipped off and there still would have been plenty of clearance to press out the old bushing.

the first day I worked on it, the bushing had only moved out about 1/4". i sprayed both sides of the bushing shell with PB Blaster and let it soak overnight in hopes that it would loosen it up. perhaps my bushings were unusually rusty but i can't see why they would be since the undercarriage of the car is virtually rust-free.

the next morning I resumed tightening the extractor tool shaft and things went a lot better. the old bushing came out the rest of the way quite easily so soaking the bushing shell in penetrant overnight did the trick. I then cleaned up the rusty surface of the bushing hole in the trailing arm using a Scotch-Brite pad and sandpaper. I used a little PB Blaster to lube the surface of the trailing arm bushing hole and the new bushing went in like a dream.

after removing the drivers' side bushing i found the manufacturer's instruction video for using this tool on YouTube. they both remove the old bushing and install the new one working from the outside of the car toward the middle of the car. this makes things a LOT easier but i don't know if the Honda/Acura trailing arm bushings or the hole they go in on the trailing arm are tapered (the instructions for some aftermarket bushing inserts claim the bushing shell outer diameter is tapered). if there is a taper i'm not sure it would be a good idea to remove and install bushings from the same direction. i looked at the Honda/Helms detailed service manual but it doesn't give any detail on trailing arm bushing removal and installation.

after spraying the passenger side bushing many times with PB Blaster and letting it soak in i tried removing it as shown in the manufacturer's YouTube video (pressing the bushing in from the outside toward the center of the car. one of the arms of the tool broke off below where it attaches to the cross brace.

i sent the broken tool back to the manufacturer and they sent me a replacement about a week and a half later with no hassles. i tried to use it on the passenger side bushing again but found that it would not fit over the edges of the trailing arm because they got distorted when i used the tool that broke. i then gave up and removed the trailing arm from the car. this was very easy to do by releasing the parking brake cable and disconnecting the brake hose from the hard brake line and plugging the line. i was able to easily remove the bushing using a hammer and punch and replaced it after cleaning up the hole it goes in.

bottom line is that on my '97 Del Sol it would have been MUCH easier to just remove the trailing arms to replace the bushings.

UPDATE: A year and a half later I used the replacement tool to replace the bushings on my '93 Civic. After reviewing a Honda Tech Bulletin I both removed the old bushings and installed the new ones from the outside of the car toward the middle of the car. ##This tool worked great.##

I had to remove the toe-adjusting bolts at the inner end of the compensating arms because the bolts at the outer ends of the compensating arms would not budge. Just make sure you outline the position of the bolt head (using paint) in the slot before you remove it so you can return it to the proper position when done replacing the bushings.

I still don't know why I had such a hard time removing the bushings in my Del Sol but I think this tool will usually work fine.

title: Good solution for minor scratches
text:
For a perfect repair, take your vehicle to a body shop. To save hundreds of dollars and lots of time, this is an excellent fix for superficial scratches and chips.

I have used other OEM touch up paints in the past. This dispenser works better than any I used in past years. The pen tip makes it easy to put a tiny amount of paint where it is needed.

For the best result apply several light coats over a period of a few days. Sand off any rough sections of paint with 600 grit (or similar) sandpaper and clean the area with a little alcohol and paper towel. It would be good to sand lightly between repeated coats (giving plenty of time to dry before sanding). Get the paint on any bare metal before there is a chance for any corrosion. If there is any possibility of rust starting, sand the exposed metal to remove it.

Best practices call for covering this with a clear coat after done painting. That will give the best appearance and durability, but is optional.

The color matches Toyota Quicksand as used on my 2016 Tacoma.

title: Essential Items if you do your own oil changes on Toyotas
text:
My 2016 Toyota Tacoma has the new oil filter design using a paper filter inside the filter housing. It, unfortunately, has as standard the plastic version of the filter housing. I could not remove the filter housing by any method until I bought this wrench. The filter was too snug, and it was plain that all my other filter wrenches were going to destroy the plastic filter housing before they would get it off. Even with this wrench it took a lot of effort to remove the filter housing -- it seemed as if there may be a slight mis-match on the filter housing threads -- but it was doable.

The drain tool seemed unnecessary and an expensive addition to buying the wrench alone-- the replacement filter came with a little disposable plastic tool that was supposed to accomplish the same thing, but was completely ineffective. It was nice to be able to drain the oil from the filter housing before loosening it, that eliminated the oil spill that normally would happen with a filter change. The plastic tube is too long unless you are lifting the vehicle a couple feet off the ground, but it can be cut to the length needed, or even removed and discarded.

If you have a Toyota that uses the paper cartridge in the filter housing that is compatible with this wrench I recommend that you either buy this set, or plan to pay a mechanic who has the proper tools to do your oil changes.

title: Yet another poorly designed spout
text:
I knew that these were slow to pour, but even so I was surprised when I timed it. It took a full 7 minutes and 58 seconds to put 5 gallons of fuel in my tank. The automatic-shutoff design of the spout is such that it allows little more than a trickle of fuel to pass. I have better things to do than idle away the afternoon fueling my equipment.

If you are dispensing fuel into anything other than a gas tank with the reduced hole for unleaded fuel you likely will find that the hook on the side of the spout slips off the edge of the fill tube, entirely stopping the flow of fuel until the hook is re-set.

I do give Midwest a point for a well-proportioned tank. It is compact with its rectangular shape and vertical sides, and wide enough to be more stable than some so it is less likely to tip over in the back of your truck.

I tried to use the old spout off a Blitz can, but there is just enough difference in the thread that the Blitz cap will not work on the Midwest can, and the diameter of the Blitz spout is a little too large to fit in the Midwest cap.

title: Excellent value
text:
I bought this to use with a Husky 2000 lb jack, http://www.amazon.com/Husky-30775-A-Frame-Wind-Trailer/dp/B004OK5SZE. That jack has a 2" diameter tube. If your jack has a different diameter, this may not be a good choice.

The dimensions shown in the description are wrong. It is not "6 x 6 x 6 inches" (and you probably would not want it if it was) but rather is approximately 2.25" wide, 4.5" long, and 1.5" tall. When parking my trailer on soft soil I will put a larger board under the jack foot to keep it from sinking in, but that is something I have always done. On packed crushed rock, pavement, or even firm sand this is fine by itself.

The stamped metal is well formed and measures approximately 1/8" thick, quite adequate for my needs.

I noticed on the manufacturer's website that the MSRP is a few pennies less than it is selling for here, so you might save a little if you pick one up locally. Nevertheless, I feel that it is an excellent value, and does what one expects from a jack foot.

Update 09/25/2022: After more than 8-1/2 years of use and abuse the foot fell off the trailer jack. It had rusted through on the sides, although the bottom plate remained solid, if rusty. Somewhat to my surprise, the bottom of the jack was in great condition. The foot obviously protected it from all the rocks and other objects snagged by the jack. I will need to use a grinder to cut off the bolt that attached the foot to the jack, but I am ordering another one of these. I thought it was an excellent value when bought in January 2014, after 8-1/2 years of faithful service I think that assessment was correct.

title: Excellent Value in an A-Frame Trailer Jack
text:
I had been watching the jack on my trailer tongue deteriorate for years and had been dreading the labor and expense to replace it. When it failed completely, I had to act. I was surprised how easily the old jack came out. I was prepared with my impact driver but once I broke the rust from the old bolts with a chisel they came out easily with a socket wrench. (Of course, your results may vary depending on how rusted your bolts are.) I measured the holes and old jack, and checked the specs at [...]. The specs showed this 2000 lb jack was an exact match, so I took a chance and ordered. It arrived, slipped right in, and the bolt holes were a perfect match with the tongue. It took about 5 minutes for the installation. The most difficult part was propping up the tongue while tightening the bolts. (Remember to buy new bolts and washers for the installation.)

I also purchased a Curt 28270 Jack Foot, http://www.amazon.com/Curt-28270-Jack-Foot/dp/B004QEH1QW, and it was quick and easy to attach that.

I am sure there are better made trailer jacks than this, but I can replace this 2 or 3 more times for the cost of one of those top quality jacks. In light of the value this jack delivers, it earns 5 stars. If ever my experience indicates otherwise, I will revise my review. Just remember to check the dimensions at the link above to be sure this is the right one for you, too.

title: Excellent value, perfect replacement
text:
One always wonders when purchasing a non-OEM part whether it really will fit. I could not find the lights I needed at a local wrecking yard, so I took a chance and ordered a pair of these taillights for my 1998 Nissan Frontier. One metal mounting bracket was slightly bent out of alignment when I received them, but that was easily straightened. They popped right into place and bolted securely with the original bolts.

These are sold without bulbs. That should not be an issue because you probably will re-use the original bulbs unless burned out or damaged. You should be aware, however, that the plastic bulb sockets and wiring from your taillights will need to be re-used with these. If you have extensive damage you may need to arrange for replacement bulb sockets and wiring, but if you just have cracked lenses there is no reason not to re-use those parts, and it simplifies installation to re-use them.

The parts of the original taillight that were metal are also metal on this replacement. The plastic appears slightly different, but I cannot say if that is due to aging of the original, or if these have a slightly different composition. I found no reason for concern about the construction of these.

The Amazon Parts Finder to "Make Sure It Fits" claims these are not a replacement for my 1998 Frontier. That undoubtedly is because these have the smoked, rather than clear, lens for the backup and turn signal lights which Nissan adopted with the 1999 model year. Anyone with a '98 Frontier should buy a pair if you want your taillights to match. Fortunately (?) both of mine were cracked (although only one was being rejected by the safety inspector) so it was easy for me to decide to replace both.

The cost to buy a pair of these was roughly half what it would have cost to buy just one OEM taillight, and replacements out of a wrecking yard would have cost more if I could have found them. So, considering the great savings and perfect fit I conclude that these lights do everything I hoped, and rate them a 5. The only tool needed to remove the old and install these was a 10mm wrench, and even the mechanically challenged should be able to handle the job. If you can change a burned out taillight bulb, you can replace the entire taillight. The only thing I find strange is that the cost differs from the left to the right taillight.

title: 2005 Tundra Install - Malfunctioning Computer? Door Lock - OK.  Alarm System - Failure
text:
Had this system installed on my 2005 Tundra. The alarm chirps, doors lock with a press of the lock button. The two doors unlock with a press of the unlock button. As a keyless remote system, this does its job.

Where it falls short is with a press of the buttons on the key fob, the alarm computer fails to activate any of the parking/brake/head lights, car horn (separate from the included alarm siren). The alarm system fails to activate when doors open. My unit does not operate as an alarm system in any regard.

The installer says, after troubleshooting the install, the computer does not appear to be activating the alarm functions. I told him to leave it installed because my primary concern was having a keyless entry system, vs. an operating alarm system. The alarm sentry light does work, so the truck does appear to be protected, even if that's not the case.

The key fobs appear sturdy. They are heavy and the buttons provide a satisfying click when pressed. Sometimes it takes a few presses of the button in order to get the system to respond, however. I am not sure if that is a symptom of my malfunctioning system. The alarm chirp is a unique sound, and sufficiently loud. This could be a plus when trying to distinguish your vehicle in a large parking lot, or trying to annoy potential thieves. Although, I find the chirp pitch to be an annoying sound compared to the viper's traditional chirp, and would personally prefer that sound for my system. But I wouldn't penalize the unit for the sound of the alarm chirp alone. Its functionality is the reason, I gave 2 stars. Had I bought from a brick and mortar store, they would have replaced the alarm system on the spot, for the same price. When you provide a malfunctioning one from Amazon for them to install, they are not quite as forgiving.

title: Sags in middle & too much tension on ends.
text:
I ordered the 12'6" (12'1" Fabric) topper and installed it myself with about 30 minutes of assistance. The size was correct and the total install took about 1.5hrs. Half of that was measuring and re-measuring where I wanted to install the brackets before drilling the holes. All in all installation went well, but I won't focus too much on it because I do not recommend this topper.

When it rained on our first trip out the middle immediately sagged and collected water. I had to run the slide in to remove the pooled water. I figured I could live with this by putting some noodles, etc under the slide to give the middle some extra support. However, on our next trip (2 months after install) I noticed an odd sound from inside the trailer. After several minutes of investigation I noticed that the middle of the roller itself was sagging causing the ends to pull in. This caused too much tension on the ends and was beginning to pull the awning rail away from the trailer on the ends. My son and I had to remove the canopy there at the campsite to prevent further damage. I wish I had taken pictures but I was too worried about getting it removed.
What a waste of money. Luckily we caught it early and can re-attach the awning rail with new butyl tape and slightly larger screws. I had such high hopes for this topper. Very disappointing.

title: Rattles at high speeds
text:
I bought one for my 2010 Cherokee. It does work some what, and looks good, but at higher speeds +70 it rattles around a bit. I have made it as tight as possible. The bottom legs that support it are very cheap plastic that only sit on the roof of the car. The entire Fairing is only held in place on top onto the actual roof rack bar, so there is no support on the bottom or sides, it only connects on the top so it can almost flip upwards and moves around a little bit. The bottom support legs come with padded stickers to sit on the roof- I can't imagine those holding well oafter a few years of rain, snow, wind etc...But who knows?

Also, if you have a sunroof and want to open it up, the sliding sunroof will be scraping the bottom leg supports which simply sit upon the roof of the car, or top window.

I'd still buy it but I think for the $ they could come up with a better connection to keep the fairing more solidly in place that what they have. I would have given 2 stars but part of the problem is that the Cherokee roof rail/rack system is pretty bad as well and very difficult to work with.

I deal with this, by using a different type of lug bolt -  an acorn spline tuner head, which means a thief will need two different specialised tools. title: Excellent Rectifier needs a critical circuit mod
text: This solid state rectifier is my preferred replacement for any vacuum tube rectifier.  None of the other reviews I have read mentions a CRITICAL piece of advice that is printed on the back of the very small owner's advice packed in with the Yellow Jacket - If simply plugged in in place of a vacuum tube rectifier, the high voltage DC in your amp will come on instantly. however your power tubes are not ready for that.  Full DC voltage on power tubes with cold cathodes will damage them.  Solution?  Install a "standby" switch to allow a warmup time, maybe 30 to 60 seconds, so that the other tubes' cathodes will be already hot when the DC voltage from the Yellow Jacket comes on.  The details of that will be easy for any good old-time electronics geek: if you are not one, find a friend who is.  On my amp, I installed a two-pole switch on both sides of the 670 volt AC transformer winding that feeds the two anodes of the rectifier tube.

My thinking was that these sides would lock the lumber in and keep them from slipping loose when transported.

With the ubiquitous Harbor Freight 20% off coupon, I could have saved about 12$ bucks with the Harbor Freight model, but otherwise they were about the same price, and the “goal post” sides were worth it to me to prevent the liability of my lumber from falling off in the street. It has worked beautifully for me. I’ve made two trips to the big box store and have hauled 16 foot boards with no problem. The only issue is that when the “goal posts” are spread out as wide as the can go, there’s a little bit of rock back and forth. I have countered this by spreading the load out as far as possible.

title: Convenent device, feels light, some mismatched labeling
text:
I ordered this to have in case of an emergency. I don't know if or when I will need to jump a car, so I'm reviewing it without having actually jump started anything. I will take the word of other reviewers that it works for that.
It is a nice size and simple to use. The LED light is not much, but would he helpful in an absolute emergency in the dark. That's not what this product is about anyway.
It is simple to charge, and to connect a USB to use it as a power bank. Also simple to use as a jump starter Per the instructions, you just plug the cables into this, connect them to the battery, start the car, and then disconnect. it all straightforward - plug in a USB-C cable to charge it, use the jumper cables to jump, or a USB-A (common USB) cable to charge other devices with this device turned on.
I like the display that shows the precise battery percentage.
This unit is light - I had expected to feel something packed with batteries, but this is not. If I did not see it in other reviews, I might be skeptical that it would jump a car.
It does not include a case or bag to keep the device and cables together.
Interestingly, the listing for the device that I ordered and received says it is 1500 peak Amps and 14,000 mAh, but there is a sticker on the box that indicates it is 2000 Amps and 20,000 mAh. Since the labeling directly on the device and in the manual does not specify either way, I am not sure which is accurate. I am assuming that the lower numbers are correct.

In summary, these work fine and I have had no problems. However, in my opinion, they provide no visible advantage over the original bulbs.

title: Works welll, but no memory. Defaults to Bars every time.
text:
[[VIDEOID:3aac4cd083648cb6d69a2ad0b025ecff]] This pump is nice and small. It's about 4 inches square. It contains all of the accessories you need, but no case for them. I think I will keep it in the box. It works fine, and can be set to the desired inflation pressure. You can choose settings tuned to inflating car tires, motorcycles, bikes, or balls.
I wanted a small rechargeable pump like this to keep in my car for emergencies. For example, if I am on a road trip and discover a slow leak in a tire, I could use this pump to safely make it to my destination and then get the tire repaired. What is annoying about the pump though, is that it doesn't remember settings when it is turned off. It always comes on set to inflate a car tire to 2.5 Bar. No cars in the US specify tire pressure in bars. You have to change it to PSI, and then set the correct pressure. In an emergency, I don't want to have to try to remember that I need to long press the "R" button in order to change the pressure to bars. I would like to set this to inflate to 35 PSI, and have it automatically return to that the next time I turn it on, but that is not possible. If I haven't used it in a while, I will be reading the tiny instructions to get the settings right. And depending on the circumstances, that could be difficult. I would have given five stars if not for this issue. If it's not going to have a memory, at least default to PSI.
It's seems to be a good little device so far other than that issue. It will be convenient for the purpose I ordered it for (to keep in my car on trips), and I will make a note to keep with it to remind me of how to easily get the settings I need. I have used it to top off several tires as the cold weather arrived. It inflated six tires from about 26 PSI to 30.5 PSI, and still had 1-2 bars left on the battery. It was down to one, but rebounded to two.
Functionally it is great. It works, the battery lasts, and it will not leave you stranded. I might look for a similar option that remembers settings, though - if you can find one at this price.

title: Work perfectly, but too bright for low beams
text:
First off, these bulbs do what they say. They fit to replace H11 halogen bulbs, they are easy to install, and they work perfectly in my Nissan Pathfinder. They even include nice gloves so that you can avoid contaminating the LED, which can shorten it's life as it gets super hot. The only downside to installation is that the bulb connects to a wire that has a plastic box containing electronics. You can see this in the pictures. You just need to find a way to stow or secure that little box so it doesn't bounce around under the hood.
As advertised, these lights are extremely bright. I installed them as low beams, and they actually illuminate better than my halogen high beams. I have included a couple of photos after installing only one so that you can see a comparison of these with the standard halogen headlights.
So everything that these bulbs advertise seems to be true, except the claim of "No Blinding Oncoming Vehicles." Of course something this bright being used in a housing that is designed for something far dimmer is going to be a problem. I should have thought of this before I ordered, but, to be honest, I didn't believe they would be as bright as advertised. Turns out they are.
Immediately after installing I noticed that they were too bright for me to be comfortable inflicting them on other drivers. I then did a test with my wife in another car. We found them to be blinding when coming toward you, and maddening when behind you. We had to dim the rear view mirror, but also turn away the side view mirror when these lights were on the car driving at a normal distance behind us.
I have since done some research, and it appears that federal regulations limit headlights to 3000 lumens. I believe that these (and probably all other similar LED retrofit bulbs) are technically illegal. That's not to say that you would be ticketed - I highly doubt that would happen. I suspect that I would have technically been breaking the law with these, but would have never had any issues due to that.
If you are OK with having the brightest lights possible at the expense of other drivers, then these are a good choice. They would also work well offroad, or anywhere that you do not encounter other traffic. I suspect that all of the bright LED retrofit bulbs have all of the downside that I mentioned. And these are good bulbs - easy to install, and bright as advertised.
For me, I am buying a new set of halogens and using them. I will keep these in case I ever need spares in an emergency while I am out. I will also use some similar LEDs to replace my high beams, since those are off when traffic is present. It is nice to turn the night into daylight in front of you, but my personal choice is to be more courteous and safe to others.
Again, I want to be clear that if you want the brightness and are choosing among the selection of LED bulbs, then I would recommend these. They do what they say, and seem high quality. The only potential downside in that respect is the little box connected to them that you should secure somewhere. It turns out that retrofitting with super bright bulbs is just not for me, though. And I also docked a star since "No Blinding Oncoming Vehicles" is included in the product description, and I saw the reality with my own eyes.

title: Outshines anything I have tried
text:
I am no professional detailer, and do not claim to have their level of knowledge. I have always waxed my cars to keep them looking nice and to protect their finish. I grew up using Rain Dance wax, and waxing my family's car or my own almost weekly during the summer. I have tried many other waxes/polishes since then. Again, I am no professional, but my favorite to this point had been Nu Finish. It shines pretty well, and the protection lasts quite a while. It is important to me to use something that is not abrasive, as I do not like scratches or swirls. Based on my experience, Nu Finish has little abrasiveness, if any.
I bought a new car recently. I asked the dealer not to detail it, as I have seen dealers buff tiny scratches and swirls into brand new cars more than once. So they just washed it and I took it home. I wanted to be sure that I protected the paint with a good wax. I required zero abrasives for this brand new car, and wanted something that would not leave white stains on black trim (Nu Finish stains any dark plastic unpainted trim that it touches, and I do not have the patience to tape things off before waxing). That research led me to Meguiar's Ultimate. I bought it locally rather than at Amazon because I needed it the same day.
I waxed the car yesterday, and am thrilled with the results. I washed the car first, of course, being careful to get it completely clean. It was 55-60 degrees and sunny - I waxed the car in the garage. The wax went on and off relatively easily. Meguiar's includes an applicator and one microfiber towel with the kit. I used those plus some extra microfiber towels. As advertised, the wax wiped off of plastic trim and tires (where I overlapped these accidentally) without staining.
The shine is unlike anything I have seen. The car truly does look wet. You can get an idea of it in the pictures I have included. If you are someone like me who wants a shiny, protected finish on your car, but are not going to spend time and money on a multi-step detailing process with professional products, then I highly recommend Meguiar's Ultimate. It is non-abrasive and non staining, so it does no inadvertent harm. And it outshines anything I have used.
I cannot yet speak to longevity since I just waxed the car yesterday. I will revisit this review in the future with an update on how this product hold us as compared to others I have used.

title: Perfect little tool for its purpose
text:

The little keyring piece pulls off to expose the seatbelt cutter and to allow you to use the glass punch. You have to pull hard, especially the first time, but this is fine because you would not want it to fall off accidentally. You just grab the ring (or the key you put on it) and pull. I have no trouble with it, and with the adrenalin of an emergency it would be even easier.

The glass punch works well and I am certain that it would easily shatter a window. You just hold the yellow body, press the black punch against the window and push hard. It makes a snap that will shatter the glass. Do not test this by pushing the black punch against your thumb or finger - that will hurt. It works over and over, and there is no trick to it.

The whistle works well with or without the keychain removed. It is louder than I expected based on other reviews. My cat does not like it.

The light is a single small LED that would help out in finding a keyhole or in a dire emergency, but is not designed to be a general use flashlight.

The entire device is smaller than I imagined. It is small enough to actually use as a keychain, but I am just keeping one in each car. About the size of a typical car entry remote.

Overall quality seems very good. I have tested all aspects several times. The battery for the flashlight is preinstalled, and an extra is included. Only the LED light function requires a battery.

These are shipped loose in an envelope with no instructions. I think that a lot of the negative comments would not have occurred if instructions were included.

text:
Great deep tone on my big block Chevy. Noticeable increase in low end torque; those big exhaust pulses need room to leave.

Exhaust sound is far more than just the muffler, so the rest of my system is 3" pipes off each cylinder bank, combined with a dual 3" to single 4" Y-pipe, then this 4" in/out muffler, and single 4" pipe over the rear axle and dumping out behind the wheels on the passenger side.

Very deep sound. Authoritative tone as power and rev's increase. No rasp, burble, or "thoatiness" at all, which I can't stand in a truck. A truck should sound like a train engine, not a dirt bike, and this system achieves that. Very slight drone in the cab when accelerating up hill under moderate throttle.

At first I was somewhat disappointed, as I was hoping for more of the classic Flowmaster clank sound. That sound seems to be getting stronger though, as I put miles and heat cycles on the system. Slightly louder than I expected, but isn't obnoxious. Definitely no worse than a straight piped Duramax or Powerstroke.

title: Not sure this is an improvement over a standard funnel, but it sure costs more
text:
TL;DR at bottom.

Finally bought the highly touted Mr. Funnel, and I have to say I'm kind of let down. It's slightly too chunky to be truly convenient(and I'm using the smallest one), and the filter stand in the middle of the funnel splashes fuel out. My main complaint is the contaminant well in the bottom of the funnel that holds a few tablespoons of fuel when you're done. I understand that this is to hold contaminants, but now I either have to pull the nozzle off the fuel can so I can dump that fuel back into the fuel can, or dump it into the engine I was fueling, completely negating the point of having a filter. I'd deal with the cumbersome size and splashing, but the fuel well in the bottom puts me over the line as far as using this on a regular basis. I'm going back to an engine oil funnel and a piece of felt.

TL;DR: If you have legit fuel contamination issues, this is probably worth the hassle. If you don't, and are just using a filter funnel because it's best practice, this is probably not worth the trouble.

text:

Then I switched all my power equipment to battery electric. String trimmer, blower, chainsaw, mower, everything. I heat with wood, cut 3-4 cords/yr, and the battery electric chainsaw still handles 99.5% of that. My two stroke fuel usage went from a few gallons per year to less than a quart per year, for the few big cuts that needed the Stihl. I was throwing away almost all of my two stroke mix, and having trouble with pump gas(even non ethanol with Stabil) going bad and causing issues.

Ding, lightbulb above my head while walking through a local store carrying this stuff. People like me are exactly what this stuff is for! I tried, it my saw loves it, no issues.

text:

I've been running this filter on my diesel swap for ~30k miles. In that time, the filter has caught around a quart of water(only takes a teaspoon to ruin your injection pump, and pretty much any amount will cause some level of damage) and who knows how much random other rust and bugs and junk. I run the 30 micron water block element in this filter, backed up by a CAT 1R-0750(2 micron absolute) for total fuel system protection. Zero issues, easy install, relatively easy to service, wish I had installed it when I swapped in the diesel engine.

I do recommend the water-in-fuel sensor and warning light, an available accessory.

The other review mentions that this filter should include fittings. I do not agree. There is such a huge variety of installs, plumbing setups, mounting setups, and flow requirements that no matter which fittings were supplied, quite a large portion of customers would still have to source their own fittings to fit their unique install.

As such, mine is juuuuuuuuust on the edge of big enough and I do notice a restriction vs. straight piped. So, the lesson is, go bigger!

Oh, and I also pulled the drain plug and coated it with copper anti seize, and reinstalled it. This style spark arrestor does need to be cleaned/drained REGULARLY, frequently enough that the drain plug shouldn't have time to seize, but for the two minutes it took it's cheap insurance. A seized drain plug is actually a sign that the spark arrestor has not been maintained correctly, and a forest ranger doing a thorough job will be checking for this.

title: Do not buy, fatal design error
text:
The bottom of the screw terminals are completely uncovered, exposed bare metal right up against the mounting surface. Be EXTREMELY cautious if mounting this fuse block on a conductive surface, as any raised area or imperfection in the surface(very common in fender wells, where this will frequently be used) will raise the mounting surface into contact with the terminal screws. Even just tightening the mounting screws too much could do so. At least it's on the outside fused leg of the circuit, where in theory all it'll do is blow the fuses? Really irresponsible to build a fuse block this way.

If you use this, make sure you mount it on a nonconductive surface, or use a nonconductive backer, but I would recommend simply not buying.

title: Holy hearing loss, Batman!
text:
Ridiculously, awe inspiringly, tinnitus-causingly, hearing damagingly loud.

Do NOT test your install by asking your helper to hit the horn button while you have your head under the hood, unless you want to be reduced to shouting "WHAT??" to communicate for the rest of the day. Won't do that again.

Do make sure you use the relay, a fuse, and solid wiring off the battery. I tried just hooking it to the stock horn wiring and got about stock horn volume. This thing draws some juice, stock horn wiring is usually pretty mediocre and you get some voltage drop when pulling this much power. Wiring straight from the battery(and a fuse) through the included relay reduced voltage drop to nil and yielded a MUCH louder horn.

I'm actually kinda looking forward to the next time someone is paying more attention to their phone than their driving and drifting into my lane.

When your Solara awning fails to retract after a long weekend, you will wish you had an old manual awning that always worked. Particularly when you wonder how you will get home with an extended awning that takes a drill and an 8 foot ladder that you don't have to retract manually.

After you take a trip or two and the speakers fall out of your Solara awning you will hope that water intrusion will not cause hundreds of dollars of damage.

After the cheap plastic covers fall off and you find out that they charge $30.00 for a $2.00 part, you will wish that the RV manufacturer would not have put the cheap crap on your $100,000 rv.

After pulling into camp with the sun blaring down, you don't extent your Solara awning because it may not retract and you might not get home you will begin to think that spending hundreds of dollars to replace the Solara piece of crap might be worth it.

title: 10 Years Old and  Still Going Strong
text:
I just returned from a 2 1/2 week boat trip and used mine as a freezer. It was set at o degrees, and when running, held a constant +3 to - 3 degrees on an outside, covered cockpit. I ran it exclusively in 110v on either shore power, generator, or on an inverter. When at anchor and unplugged and kept closed the temperature raised to no more than 25 degrees in the morning.

I also use it on road trips in my pickup truck. It was necessary to run a fairly heavy cable to the battery from a 12v socket under my canopy. With undersized wire, the voltage would drop and the chest would shut itself off in order to protect the battery.

Mine is approximately 10 years old (I don't remember where we got it), and is labeled "Edgestar." It looks just like this one, both inside and outside

We also use it as a supplemental refrigerator during the holidays and with company (and when cleaning/defrosting our home refrigerator and freezer. It spends most of the time stored and off in our garage.

Pros - It works. It is capable of a range of cold settings, including well below freezing. It is sturdy, has good hinges, handles and a latch. It keeps cold, like an ice chest, when not plugged in. It is also very quiet.

Cons - It is heavy (empty) with a significant amount of interior space dedicated to it's machinery. It's feet are steel with rubber pads that are sticky - good most of the time, bad for moving, or sliding on the floor. My 12v plug has a nipple that broke off and had to be glued back from misuse, not poor construction. I find the settings confusing enough that I keep a pdf manual on my phone in order to remember the mystery button sequence it takes to set the dang thing.

title: It struggled but did the job when needed
text: I wouldn't trust this without a full charge on it.  I've started a classic car with a super dead battery (a 1960's "compact car") had to use the override and I'm scary so I had to get advice from my cousin.  That was 2 years ago.  Fast forward to last week I had a dead battery in my daily driver and had to get a jump from a coworker,  I should've been carrying this but afraid that the Florida heat would kill it.  It's been in a climate-controlled house.  Took the Noco out again and topped off the charge (which didn't take but an hour to be certain) for the next expected dead battery morning.  Compared to a similar sized jumper that was used at an auto parts store (I went to get the battery tested), the Noco wasn't strong.  On a 2 door 5 cylinder hatchback with a battery that can't hold a charge (basically dead), it took 2 attempted cranks, both had 30 seconds before the attempt to get the car running, and it still sounded like it took added effort. I mean it saved me time and I didn't need assistance, and I felt safe using a device like this (I'm scary about jumping vehicles from past sparking experiences).  But if you have larger needs like turning over a truck or something that takes a larger jump than a subcompact car, this ain't guaranteed to start it.

title: The electric plug support is wonky, but the rest of the bracket is fine
text:
I have this installed on my travel trailer’s to ngue jack shaft. Installation was pretty simple but does require two wrenches/sockets due to the fasteners used, versus using a carriage bolt or similar. It’s made of mild steel that you basically bend around your mounting point, then is friction-secured using a bolt and nut. It does stay in place just fine. The included trailer plug cover fits snugly and I expect it to last one year or so as the tether will probably fail first.

The only bad part is the retainer for the trailer plug, which is a piece of elastic cord. The idea is that the elastic cord will hold the cable below the plug snug against the post or mount. This just plain doesn’t work well and I end up with my cable pulled farther through and flipping in the air (but at least it’s off the ground). The elastic cord is already stretched out after one month, and I expect total failure before the end of summer. I’d rather there be some extension of the steel bracket, a horizontal version of the vertical metal arms that hold the chains.

More pros than cons, but I wish I had searched longer for a better product.

title: Absolute fail on the first try

I bought this to try with an existing crimp handle that they wouldn’t at all fit. The next day I ordered the proper tool to use it with. I inserted the first steel (not stainless) fastener in some 20 gauge sheet metal pulled slowly but deliberately on the crimp handles, and had them suddenly let go with the feel and sound of the fastener stripping. Tried a second fastener from a different batch (some came with the tool and I ordered extra), and had the same result. I switched to the die that came with the new handle, and it worked like a champ.

I looked at this insert, and could see just a little bit of shiny metal where the threads let go. I also noticed the threads are really shallow, and it was really obvious when comparing with the new tool. In fact, I was able to use the fasteners that this set couldn’t compress using the new tool, with zero problems.

title: This stuff works!
text:
Was made aware of this stuff while watching a video on the YouTube channel Tested (with Adam Savage). His recommendation and product demonstration convinced me to order a gallon jug of it.

Main reason I wanted something like this was to de-rust an old adjustable wrench I had - a tool I inherited from my father. It had gotten left under the kitchen sink and some how got wet - which resulted in it being completely rusted solid. I've tried different things over the years to clean the rust off of it and out of the works - but had no success. I had pretty much given up. So when I saw the video, I thought why not give this a try - the price of a gallon was fairly inexpensive. So I order a gallon jug.

I can say the results were beyond my expectations - after soaking in this for 24 hours - all the rust was gone. I did have to use a small wire brush to clean up the works that adjusted the opening on the wrench - but that was a minimum amount of effort. The wrench almost looks brand new.

I'm more than happy with my purchase of this rust remover and recommend it.

title: Something every car should have
text:
Over the years I've had a number of different kinds of these devices and think there should be one in the trunk of everybody's car. I've been driving around without one lately. I had loaned my previous one to a co-worker to use and he some how managed to drive over the nozzle and broke it. So I was happy to get to try out one of these compact units. The day before I was to receive the compressor I ran over something on my way to work and ended up having to take my car into the tire place I use. I had apparently run over some sort of screwdriver and it pierced the tire. Still, it was a slow leak and I was able to get to the shop before the tire went flat. But all the way there I was worried I wouldn't make it and would have to pull over on the side of a busy road and deal with changing out the tire for the spare. If I had this compressor I wouldn't have worried as much.

Today (weeks later) I came out to get in my car to go to work and found I had a flat (that same tire that had been fixed). Figured it would be a good chance to test the compressor. This has to be the smallest tire compressor I've ever used. I have to say it worked adequately. Taking it out of the box and unwinding the power cord was pretty intuitive. The power cord is long enough to reach both the front & back tire locations - as long as you use the car doors on the side with the tire needing air. I was surprised to find that this unit doesn't use the typical bayonet style connector, but instead has a screw on connector. I screwed on the hose connector finger tight. Turning on the compressor is done with the single button on the front of the device. The compressor makes a bit if noise as the air pump runs and vibrates - which is typical of air compressors. I like that there is a pressure gauge built-in to the face of the unit, made it easy to know when to turn off the compressor. The gauge is marked with shading to show the typical rAnge of air pressure for most passenger cars - but, that shading is red, so I might wonder that some people might think that was indicating Danger. This compressor lived up to the claim on the box that it could fully inflate a tire in about five minutes. That's about all the time it took me from start to finish before I was on the road heading to the tire shop to get my tire looked at. I am happy to have this compressor in my car, it's one less thing to worry about.

title: Loose locks
text:
This works for me. I usually oil the locks around my house once a year - using [[ASIN:B0083V8LPO 3-IN-ONE Multi-Purpose Oil]]. So I was happy to get a sample can of this aerosol version. It worked just as well and was easier to apply. I used it on more than just locks - I also sprayed all the hinges on the outside of my house. If you got a outside lock (or a hinge) I would recommend either style product.

I did have an issue with the little red straw that comes with the can. It comes attached to the can with a piece of tape - after detaching (and using the product) I wrapped a rubber-band around the can and used that to secure the straw during storage. I should mention that I lost the straw for awhile (took me forever to find it). I had just sprayed the lock on one of the outside burglar-bars on the back of my house and the straw had disappeared. Thinking it had just fell out of the nozzle I searched the ground & grass under the window. Five minutes of searching and no straw to be found. Eventually found it, long-story short, when I was spraying the lock the straw came loose and was propelled by the oil and the straw was shot about 20 feet away. I mention this as I'm probably not the only person that's happen to.

title: Works as advertized

Many users of other lights and some of this one complain about the light pattern not being focused on the road. For me, on the contrary. Even if I used these in a reflector (not projector with lens), the light beam was too narrow horizontally and a bit too wide vertically. For my high beam, I would prefer the opposite. And we cannot rotate the light bulb in the H7 clip socket.
The same seller has another option for H7 that allows separate installation of the collar, but that one has the bulb assembly too long for my specifics and I could not close the dust cover on it.
This light gave about two times better brightness compared to the halogen bulb, and the color temperature was about 5000K-5500K. No canbus error, no flickering. Unfortunately due to the light pattern for my application I had to return it.

title: I see these being called "NO Drill" flares, they are not
text: If you are able jack up the truck and remove the wheels, I put these on my 04-08 line f150. There are 2 points on each wheel well where factory holes can be tapped and since each flare gets 5 plugs that means you need to drill 12 holes in all. I have a right angle drill and it worked out fine but if you don't take the wheel off. The way the adhesive strips are laid out some have no backing in large areas, this is just a lousy way to save plastic I guess but you need to fold those parts out and clip them in place ahead of the install day. This will help force those spots to meet metal instead of just folding under and attaching to the air, poor design. Not marked and no instructions so pay attention to the body lines and match up the tabs to the body that way, it's like a little notch/tab match game but front-rear-left-right are all similar but the notch is only filled one way. It will make more sense in hand, once you go in knowing what I learned on my truck the end product is by far the closest to factory flares i have found. They could fix some obvious short comings and have a great product but its still very usable with the minor tweaks . Important part*** they use automotive 3M tape, it needs a couple days to really take hold, dont install on hot days, try to avoid parking in direct sun for hours for a couple days (48hours min.) and avoid things like car washes, or any powerful water stream until fully cured. Follow these tips and you will end up with a great install and they do look great!

title: Quality and price make for a great set of tips!
text: These are very nice tips for the price, overall an excellent replacement for my old rusted tips. They are wide, 3.5" on the output end, make sure you have the clearance between your bumper or body if your existing tips are smaller. I can say if I had bought 4" tips I would have had a problem getting them on. They are a nice tight fit for 2.25" pipes, the clamping system is a Torx style bolt head, much better and easier to tighten than a Philips or flathead screw that tend to strip over time, nice deep head. The fit is tight enough that you need to tighten the clamp much at all, which is a good thing because I do see the possibility of breaking the clamp mount by over tightening it. Not a real issue if bought to fit 2 1/4" pipes, they even have a small drain hole drilled at the bottom of the tip end, it just speaks to the quality of the design. I can honestly say I got exactly what I wanted from this purchase, they have the weight of T304 steel, time will tell if they are rust proof but I gave them a good coat of silicone spray which also aids in getting them to slide onto older pipes. 5 stars!

text: After trying this new charger on an 5 year old red top optima group 65 and a 5 year old complelety discharged blue top optima deep cycle group 65,And a 3 year old mazda factory installed battery(group 35)standard lead acid battery.The red top was still working to start my 8 cylinder van and the blue top was dead because of a failed battery isolator.The blue top is a deep cycle used as a second battery in my van for back up power.The mazda battery came out of a 2012 mazda 3 that belongs to my sister,That just started showing signs of failure.First up is the red top.I used a new autometer battery analyzer to check the cca-voltage-and relative charge automatically compensating for temperature with estimated battery temp supplied by you the user during input stage.So after inputting the battery cold cranking amps rating(which is 800)-general temperature of the battery(70deg).The battery tested marginal with 500 cca at 12.6volts.After using agm mode to fully charge battery to float charge level(which took about 4 hours to fully charge from 80%).Battery tested out at 560 cca at 12.8volts.discharged battery to 70% and charged in reconditioning mode.Battery got slightly warmer and charged up in about 5 hours to float level.Retested battery 560cca and 12.8volts.No increase in capacity.The blue top was even worse,Voltage started at 4.2volts and took 12 to 14 hours to reach 12 volts and another day to fully charge.Tested battery(750cca)battery came back BAD at only 100cca and 12.9volts.At no point could I get the charger to Desulfate any battery.Even the 3 year old lead acid battery recieved no benefit from the recondtion mode on the charger.This charger is a GOOD slow rate charger,That has a supply mode which is good for maintaining important memory setting when disconnecting battery.But has NO desulfating capabilities at all!Probably best used for moderate battery charging duty or as a battery maintainer that can be left on all the time,Keeping battery the fully charged at all times.

title: Finicky, but pretty
text:
Between travel-trailers, tent camping, and living on a boat for a while, we have a lot of experience with different types of portable toilet systems. Specifically, I bought this to replace a similar sized 10 yr. old Thetford with a worn out main seal. The first 3 weeks after we bought this Dometic, I would have rated it a 1 or maybe 2. Now that I've gotten used to its quirks, it isn't so bad.

My family of 5 kids has used this frequently over the past several months. The first time my 3 yr. old used it, she knocked the seal out of its track trying to flush it. This happened several times over the next few weeks -- I even did it myself once. Very difficult to put it back on its sliding track, and usually a messy process. I was going to send the thing back, but then I blinked (a month went by) and realized it hasn't happened the past dozen times we've used it. I guess we got the hang of it, but there's definitely a design flaw. One thing I noticed is the placement of the handles on the front -- there's a good, strong handle on the back of the lower unit. The front handle is on the top unit. The ~third time I picked it up (full, obviously) by the two handles, the top came off (it's only held on by a little plastic spring clip, not a sliding lever like my Thetford). Veeerrrrryyyyy irritating. I've learned to be very careful to make sure that clip is well secured and that I try to hold most of the weight with the back side handle, and not the front. Because of this and the close placement between the two, there's a tendency to grasp the front by the flush handle instead of the lift handle, but it can't handle the strain and pops out of its track, making quite a mess. Note: this was not the first time it had popped out, but probably the 3rd or 4th.

The emptying process needs some work. There is a little pressure relief valve that has to be turned -- not the most intuitive of processes, and it seems to be an unnecessary irritation. My Thetford unit has a push lever right next to the handle you use to open the ventilation port while you dump it. I might actually prefer the turn-valve, but it's too small and doesn't allow sufficient airflow, which makes the thing 'hiccup' while dumping, and the plastic turn-stops never hold it, so you have to double check to make sure it's pointing the right direction. One thing I DID like about the arrangement, the top will not go onto the bottom unless the valve is closed, thereby preventing accidentally leaving it open during use.

The seat cover securement is a little finicky. I like that it pops into place with little effort, but it's hard for my younger ones to get back open. It's stiff, and I even have to use two hands. That's nice when you're carrying it around, but annoying when you're trying to open it in the dark with one hand full of tissue paper and the other holding a flashlight.

The pressurized water flushing mechanism is excellent. The finish quality on the exterior surfaces is superb -- better than my other units. It's aesthetically pleasing, by comparison.

Overall, this is a pretty unit, and the main sections seem to made of a very high grade of plastic, but the function leaves a lot to be desired. It will do, but for $155 I really expected it to be a little more durable and easy to use. Can't say I would recommend it, for the price.

title: After 35K miles = great!
text:
Updated 7/2/18 - After about 35k miles on these tires I still like them. They have maybe 5K of tread left - good for the rest of Summer, maybe. Traction remains good, even in the rain. I did find that inflating them to 32 was plenty. Anything over that and the center tread begins to wear unevenly/first.
Original review: These Falken's went on a MINI Clubman S and we are very happy with them. They are sooooo quiet compared to the oem run flats, which were incredibly rigid causing the ride to be seriously harsh. With these tires added it was like getting new struts/shocks too; much softer. I do have them inflated to about 38 to keep some tight handling. The run flats were like a track tire in that department.
I see another reviewer made note of issues in heavy rain. We were out in fairly heavy rain today and had no problem. If there's standing water, puddling on a highway, then sure, there's gonna be some slipping. But that can happen in my pickup too. The tread pattern on these should be very good in rain (and make them unidirectional, btw). Of course the type of car, suspension, alignment, inflation and many other things contribute to handling, regardless of conditions.

title: The Little Pump That Could.
text: I built a macerator station to empty the gray and black tanks on a used RV I purchased from a private owner. The tanks were full and desperately needed cleaning, so I purchased the Surgeflo to pump the contents up hill into our septic tank. I was concerned at first because the motor seemed to drag. Once everything was connected and running, it seemed to work fine until it started to drag again and would shutoff after running for only 20 seconds, rest and automatically restart. Once the job was complete and I broke everything down to clean, I discovered why it was overheating. The pump blades were tangled in a big knot of dog hair and a chunk of hard plastic was lodged under the blades and dragging against the stainless steel wall. There was also a bottle safety stopper blocking the outlet hose, but this pump did exactly what it was designed to do, just a lot slower. The safety feature would shut the pump down when it overheated and once it cooled it would start back up. It took a while to remove and unclog the debris, but once it was clear the pump ran full speed ahead. Because of the trash in the RV sewer tanks it took a long time to clean. Now the pump is cleaned it works perfectly and 10 times faster. This little pump got a major workout and made it through. I feel confident it will serve us well for many years to come. I'll let you know.

title: You Absolutely Need One

title: Amazing and really waterproof!
text:
We purchased this based on the excellent reviews, and we weren't disappointed! We had to take a 1,000+ mile road trip from Minnesota to Virginia and it withheld amazingly even when it rained. It reduced our gas mileage a bit (as to be expected), but did not make us feel the "road sway" that pull behind trailers would have. We did have an issue parking in a garage as the overhead clearance didn't allow it. Also, I'd recommend adding a few ratcheted straps for extra security. We were able to fit two 8" twin foam mattresses rolled up in it along with a bunch of clothing.

PROS:
*Huge - able to fit 2 twin foam mattresses and extras!
*Waterproof - withstood downpours
*Secure - esp. if you add some ratchet straps

CONS:
*Reduces gas mileage about a 1-2 MPG
*Hard to fit in some parking garages

Overall, this was an excellent purchase and I highly recommend it!

title: Handy gadget for charging alone!!
text:
This portable jump starter is great. First off I have not yet used it to jump a car. However we just recently lost power to our house for several hours due to an outage. My wife and I both needed to charge our phones as this happened very late in the afternoon, and by this point we both had our phones almost drained from a days use. Enter the portable jump starter. I had just received this thing and had it laying on the table, so I grabbed it and checked to see if it had any juice. Lucky for us it was fully charged. It has a couple of USB ports and one of them is actually USB 3.0 Quick charge. So I grabbed our phone cords and plugged them into this thing and Bam it started charging our phones. The quick charge works great. It saved us from not having any way to get updates on the power and help keep us from being bored to death,lol.

It also has a flashlight as well as USB mini and USB type c ports. To charge the charger itself with. Flashlight is very bright too. The charger comes with a very nice case to keep the charger and it's cords all inside so you don't loose anything. So that was a surprise.

Overall I give this an A+, and that's with out even using it for it's main purpose yet. But if it starts car without issue it's a great tool to have and keep in a car for emergency. Heck even if it doesn't jump a car it's still a valuable tool just for the flashlight and charging ability alone.

title: Point-n-shoot thermometer, very handy and fun to point at things.
text:
I love it, but wound up not using it very much.

Here's the thing -- the device only reads back the *surface* temperature of things. It's useless for letting you know if your meat is done, or pretty much anything else you need to read the temperature for. I use it to know if the griddle is hot enough for pancakes, and that's about it. Once you've confirmed that it reads the right values for a bowl of ice water and a pot of boiling water, then what?

Also: transparent materials are an issue. When you point the device at something behind glass, are you measuring the temperature of the glass, or the thing behind it? The answer turns out to be a little of both, so open the window first. I suspect that when you point it at a pot of clear water, you're also partly measuring the temperature of the pot under the water as well as the water. Keep in mind that substances' transparency to IR light is often different from their transparency to visible light, so you can't just look at something and judge whether the thermometer is seeing the object or seeing *through* it.

One more thing: the device works by measuring infra-red radiation. Materials radiate infra-red in proportion to their temperature, AND the "emissivity" of the material. A professional quality IR thermometer would have a setting you could adjust for the emissivity of the material, but these low-end devices do not. My guess is that the emissivity is set at the factory for water. This would be because a) everybody who plays with it when they get home would test it by pointing it at water, and b) most of the things you need to measure, i.e. food, are mostly water anyway.

Still, when you just want the temperature of something, like the surface of a griddle, you can't beat it.

title: A good value for a solid wiper
text:
**** Feb 2020 Update ****
I have moved my review from 4 stars to 5 stars. I had complained about mild streaking in my original review (still listed in its entirety below). What I discovered is that my crappy old wipers left a slight residue on my windshield. Once that wore off the new wiper blades are giving me an incredibly streak free wipe. These blades perform better than the RainX blades I compared them too originally. I highly recommend this product.

Summary
If you are looking for an affordable pair of wiper blades comparable to the Rain-X Latitude these seem to be a worthy buy. I find them almost as good on all counts listed below. However, I cannot vouch for the length of life yet.

Full Review
I’ve used Rain-X latitude wipers on all my vehicles for many years and in some pretty harsh situations (I love to ski when the snow is falling). Those wipers have become my standard and for this review are what I am comparing these too. As the Rain-X wipers are getting more expensive I was looking for an alternative. The six month warranty, natural rubber, and extreme use claims of these wipers were what caught my eye. Since they came in a two pack for a very competitive price I decided to give them a shot.

Shipping - A+
Though the order was not prime eligible they did offer free shipping. It only took three business days for the order to arrive. It was neatly packed and in good shape upon arrival.

Installation - A-
There was a very nicely typed and illustrated installation guide in the box. They also have a YouTube video if that is not enough.

These were not quite as easy to install as the Rain-X latitude blades. However, once they clicked into place they were very secure and looked just fine. I did not need the video to figure it out!

Performance - A
At interstate speeds they do not clatter and flap in the wind. They stay on the windshield just like other high performance beam wipers.

I haven’t been through any rain storms yet so I simulated one with a pressure washer. The blades seemed to wipe along their entire length and were very quiet. They left some trailing air bubbles which caused some minor streaking. I also have used them on a drizzly morning and again the wipe is across the whole blade but there is minor streaking. I think the jury is still out but my initial conclusion is that they are just slightly less good than my Rain-X Lattitude wipers. However, the lower price is currently making up for the slightly lower performance.

Life - ??
I just installed these blades so I have no idea if they will hold up as claimed. Because the performance is so close to the Latitude wipers and the installation was relatively easy I think life will be the determining factor if these are the value I am hoping for. We’ll have to wait and see.
